pages.brief: At the World Trade Center site in New York City, a memorial design competition is under way. Thousands of people from sixty-three nations send in designs, and eight finalists are selected. Construction continues for nearly seven years until the memorial opens on September 11, 2011.

pages.text: The memorial in New York City has two huge pools of water where the Twin Towers once stood. The country’s largest artificial waterfalls flow into the pools, around which 2,983 names are carved. These are the names of the victims of all three September 11 attacks and another attack on the Twin Towers on February 26, 1993.
pages.brief: Two huge square pools of water sit where the Twin Towers once stood in New York City. The country’s largest artificial waterfalls flow down into the pools, and 2,983 names are carved around the edges, honoring victims of the three September 11 attacks and the 1993 attack.

pages.text: In Pennsylvania, the National Park Service held a competition to find a design for its own memorial. Over one thousand people sent in their designs, but only one was chosen. The wall is made of forty pieces of marble. Each piece of marble has the name of one passenger who died in the plane crash carved into it. The memorial wall follows the plane’s flight path to a large boulder in a field. The boulder marks the crash site.
pages.brief: In a Pennsylvania field, a memorial wall made of forty pieces of marble follows the plane’s flight path toward a large boulder. Each marble piece is carved with the name of one passenger who died in the crash. The boulder marks the crash site.

pages.text: The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, opened a memorial on September 11, 2008. It has 184 benches. The name of a victim who died at the Pentagon is carved into the end of each one. To read the names, a person must face the south side of the building, where the plane crashed. At night, bright lights shine from underneath the benches.
pages.brief: At the Pentagon memorial in Arlington, Virginia, 184 benches are arranged in a quiet outdoor space. Each bench has a victim’s name carved into its end, and a person reading a name faces the south side of the building where the plane crashed. At night, bright lights shine from beneath the benches.

pages.text: Ceremonies Every year on September 11, the people in charge of these memorials and others around the United States hold special ceremonies. People from the United States and other countries around the world come to watch and participate in them.
pages.brief: Every September 11, crowds gather at memorials across the United States for special ceremonies. People in charge of the memorials lead the events, and visitors from the United States and other countries come to watch and take part in the remembrance.

pages.text: In New York, the city turns on many bright lights that shine into the night sky where the World Trade Center towers once stood. The city also has large gatherings where people come to speak, listen, and remember.
pages.brief: In New York City at night, many bright lights shine upward into the sky where the World Trade Center towers once stood. Nearby, a large gathering of people comes together to speak, listen, and remember during a September 11 ceremony.

pages.text: At the Pentagon, military officials hold a wreath-laying ceremony. People come from all over the world to set wreaths of flowers with messages and photos around the memorial. Even the president of the United States has come.
pages.brief: At the Pentagon memorial, military officials hold a wreath-laying ceremony. People from around the world place wreaths of flowers with messages and photographs around the memorial. The president of the United States is shown among the visitors.

pages.text: At the memorial in Pennsylvania, people ring two bells, called “The Bells of Remembrance,“ every September 11 at the exact time the plane crashed. They ring the bells forty times while the name of each victim is read aloud. Similar bells travel all around the United States. People ring them at the memorials for tragic events, including other September 11 memorials, to remember those who died.
pages.brief: At the Pennsylvania memorial, people ring two bells at the exact time the plane crashed. They ring them forty times while the name of each victim is read aloud. Similar traveling bells are shown at other memorials for tragic events, where people ring them to remember those who died.

pages.text: Remembering People all over the United States and the world take time each year to remember the tragic events of September 11. They remember all the people who were impacted by the attacks and the events that followed. They remember to honor the people who were lost or sacrificed to save others. They remember so they can strive to make the United States and the world a better place for everyone.
pages.brief: People across the United States and around the world pause each year to remember the September 11 attacks. They gather in quiet reflection, honoring those who were lost and those who sacrificed to save others, and look toward making the country and the world a better place.

books.title: Mozart
books.art_why: Mozart is a named famous person, so the book uses cartoon art.

pages.text: The Toddler Pianist Leopold Mozart walked into the chapel in Salzburg, Austria, followed by his two small children. “I’d like to sign my daughter Nannerl up for music lessons. She is eight years old, and I already believe she has quite a talent for music,” he said to the organist. The organist, Anton, smirked a bit, for he knew how Leopold could boast about his children. “So, when will you be signing up the little boy?” Anton asked.
pages.brief: Leopold stands in a Salzburg chapel with Nannerl and little Wolfgang beside him, speaking to Anton the organist. Anton smirks as he listens. The chapel interior and the organist's manner are visible, with Leopold's two small children close by.

pages.text: Leopold laughed at the joke, for little Wolfgang was only three years old. “Not for at least five years—I think eight is certainly young enough. Little Wolfgang’s fingers would barely be able to stretch over the keys.” The organist promised to sign Nannerl up. Before Leopold left, the organist called Nannerl over to the church piano. “Come, I will give you a beginner lesson,” he said. Nannerl ran over to her father, and Wolfgang toddled happily after her. “Me too, Papa, me too!” he cried.
pages.brief: Leopold laughs near the chapel, while Anton calls Nannerl to the church piano for a beginner lesson. Nannerl runs to her father, and little Wolfgang toddles happily after her with his hand raised, eager to join. The church piano and the family are shown together.

pages.text: “No, no, Wolfgang, you are too small,” said his father. “Pianos are not meant for little folks to touch, so please go outside and play.” Wolfgang turned around obediently. If his father had seen the disappointed look on little Wolfgang’s face, it would have broken his heart. Wolfgang went outside and played near the door of the church, but his every thought was on the piano. After Nannerl had finished, Wolfgang and Leopold went to speak with the organist again. Wolfgang crept up to the piano and put his little hands on the keyboard. He began to play the simple scales he had heard his big sister practicing.
pages.brief: Wolfgang stands outside near the church door with a disappointed face after his father sends him out. Later, inside, he creeps up to the piano and places his little hands on the keyboard, beginning to play the scales he heard Nannerl practice. Leopold and Nannerl are nearby.

pages.text: The sound entranced him, and he played the scales over and over, playing them exactly right. He forgot everything else—he did not notice his father and sister standing behind him. He didn’t even hear his father shouting for the organist to come see. He was completely wrapped up in the music. He began changing the scales, even inventing simple tunes of his own. Leopold stared at his young son Wolfgang. The boy was a musical prodigy.
pages.brief: Wolfgang sits at the piano, absorbed in playing the scales over and over. Leopold and Nannerl stand behind him, watching, while Wolfgang does not notice them. His hands move as he changes the scales and invents simple tunes, and Leopold stares at his young son.

pages.text: The Child Wonder Mozart played music as naturally as he breathed. When he was four years old, it took him only half an hour to learn a difficult piece of music that was written down. If he heard the piece, even if he heard it only once, he could memorize it instantly. When Wolfgang was five, Leopold and a friend came in to find him bent over a piece of paper and writing big, black notes, smearing and splattering ink everywhere. “Wolfgang, what are you doing spoiling the nice, clean paper?” his father asked.
pages.brief: Wolfgang, now five, bends over a piece of paper and writes big black notes, smearing and splattering ink. Leopold and a friend find him at this work. The scene shows the messy paper and the small boy concentrating on the notes.

pages.text: “Papa, I’m writing a concerto,” Mozart said, his little eyes shining. His father picked up the paper and laughed. But soon his amusement turned to amazement. It was a concerto, composed for several instruments. He could see that the notes were correct, despite the smears and blotches. “But Wolfgang, this music would be too difficult for anyone to play,” he said. “Oh, no, it would only take some practice. See, it goes like this,” said Wolfgang, and he ran to the piano. He placed his smudged paper on the music stand and began to play.
pages.brief: Wolfgang stands with shining eyes beside his father, who holds the smudged paper. Leopold's laughter turns to amazement as he looks at the notes. Wolfgang runs to the piano, places the smudged paper on the music stand, and begins to play, showing how the concerto goes.

pages.text: His father’s friend had been laughing— he’d assumed Leopold was just playing along with Wolfgang. But now he saw that the child was a true wonder. “You ought to travel with him,” the friend suggested. “He should be playing for emperors, for kings and queens.” “Perhaps I will,” said his father.
pages.brief: Leopold's friend stands near father and son, no longer laughing. He looks at Wolfgang with wonder and gestures as he suggests that Leopold travel with the child and have him play for emperors, kings, and queens. Leopold listens and answers thoughtfully, with Wolfgang nearby.

pages.text: The following year, when Wolfgang was only six years old, he and Nannerl started on tour. Wherever Wolfgang went to play, people would giggle at him. He was so small compared to the big piano, and his feet couldn’t even touch the floor. But when he began to play, the audiences fell silent. His playing was perfect and beautiful. The first place they went to play was in Vienna, the capital of Austria. On the way, they stopped to visit a monastery in a little town. There was a great pipe organ in the chapel.
pages.brief: Wolfgang, now six, and Nannerl begin their tour. People giggle at how small he looks beside the big piano, his feet unable to reach the floor, but audiences fall silent when he plays. On the way to Vienna, the family stops at a monastery chapel with a great pipe organ.

pages.text: “I want to play on it,” Wolfgang said. “Papa, explain the pedals to me.” Wolfgang’s father helped his son onto the high stool. He was too small to even operate the pedals, so he walked across them instead. The music poured out of the chapel, growing more and more powerful. The monks, who had been at dinner, rushed into the room. Because Wolfgang was so small, the monks could not see him, and they thought the organ was playing itself. “It’s an angel!” they cried. “Such music must come from heaven!”
pages.brief: Wolfgang sits high on the organ stool while his father helps him. Too small to operate the pedals, he walks across them, and music pours through the chapel. Monks rush in from dinner and, unable to see the small boy, cry out that an angel must be playing.

pages.text: Wolfgang was also very charming. Everywhere he went, people were smitten with this little musician. The customs officials asked him why he came to Vienna. “I came to play the piano,” he said. “Why, you’re no bigger than a chicken. You can’t be old enough to play anything but a whistle.” “I’ll show you,” Wolfgang said. He asked the officials to open the box containing his piano, and the little boy began to play right in the customs house. A crowd gathered around in awe. The head of customs immediately gave the order to let the Mozart family through without difficulty.
pages.brief: At the customs house, Wolfgang stands before officials who ask why he has come to Vienna. He asks them to open the box containing his piano, then plays right there. A crowd gathers around in awe, and the head of customs gives the order to let the Mozart family through.

pages.text: After playing in Vienna, Wolfgang was invited to spend the day with the royal children. One of the princesses was the famous Marie Antoinette, who was just a little girl about Wolfgang’s age. Wolfgang liked her very much. She took him around the palace to show him all the wonderful riches. He was not used to such smoothly polished floors, and he slipped and fell. All the children laughed except Marie. After she helped him up, Wolfgang said, “When I am a man, I will marry you.” The princess’s servant gasped. Then Wolfgang put his arms around Marie and gave her a big kiss. “ Dreadful!” cried the servant, for it was never, ever allowed for a common person to touch royalty. But Marie only Wolfgang’s hand, and gave him a kiss back.
pages.brief: In the palace, Marie Antoinette leads Wolfgang through rooms of riches. He slips on the smooth floor and falls; the other children laugh, but Marie helps him up. Wolfgang puts his arms around her and kisses her, while a shocked servant gasps and cries out. Marie gives him a kiss back.

pages.text: The Poor Young Man Wolfgang, his father, and his sister toured all around Europe. Wolfgang’s fame grew, and he became a very handsome young man. But unfortunately, the life of a musician did not pay well. People were less impressed with his playing as he got older. After all, a six-year-old musician was a marvel, but a twenty-year-old musician was nothing new.
pages.brief: Wolfgang, now a handsome young man, tours around Europe with his father and sister. His fame has grown, but the life of a musician does not pay well. Audiences are less impressed with his playing now; a six-year-old musician was a marvel, but a twenty-year-old musician is nothing new.

pages.text: For his entire adult life, Wolfgang Mozart was very poor. Once, a friend came to visit him and found Wolfgang and his young wife waltzing around their apartment. They were not dancing for joy; they were dancing to try and keep warm, because they could not afford fuel. Wolfgang’s wife, Constance, was often ill. They also had little children to take care of. Everyone agreed that his music was wonderful, but writing, selling, and playing music did not bring in much money.
pages.brief: In their apartment, Wolfgang and his young wife Constance waltz together, not for joy but to keep warm because they cannot afford fuel. A friend visits and finds them dancing. Constance is often ill, and little children are in their care, while money for the family is scarce.

pages.text: The Requiem One day when Mozart was thirty-six, a tall stranger dressed in gray pounded on his door. Without saying a word, he handed Mozart an envelope. Inside was some money and an order for Mozart to write a requiem. Nothing in the envelope said whom it was for. “It is for myself,” Mozart said to Constance. “I feel it in my heart.”
pages.brief: A tall stranger dressed in gray pounds on Mozart's door. Without saying a word, he hands Mozart an envelope containing money and an order to write a requiem. Mozart speaks to Constance, telling her it is for himself and that he feels it in his heart.

pages.text: She laughed. He was only thirty-six, and it was silly for him to talk of dying! The truth was that the requiem had been ordered by a count. He wanted to play the music at his wife’s funeral, but he wanted to say that he had written it himself. But Mozart didn’t know this.
pages.brief: Constance laughs at Mozart's talk of dying, saying he is only thirty-six. The scene shows the count who secretly ordered the requiem: he wanted to play it at his wife's funeral and claim he had written it himself. Mozart does not know this.

pages.text: Wolfgang began writing. He wrote feverishly, staying up all night, sometimes even forgetting to eat. The work exhausted him, and he began to grow weak. Mozart had been making a little money by teaching music students. But now he was so wrapped up in the requiem that he cancelled all of his classes. Without money, the family couldn’t afford much food. They couldn’t afford candles to light their cold house at night. But still Mozart wrote, growing weaker and weaker. Finally, just before finishing the requiem, Mozart died. It truly had been his own requiem.
pages.brief: Mozart writes feverishly through the night, staying up and forgetting to eat. The work exhausts him, and he grows weaker. He has cancelled his music classes, so the family cannot afford much food or candles. Still he writes on, growing weaker and weaker, until he dies just before finishing the requiem.

pages.text: The Greatest Musician Who Ever Lived Mozart is still considered the greatest musician who ever lived. But when he died, his family was so poor they could not purchase a gravestone. Eventually, no one could remember where he had been buried. Today there is a great monument to Mozart in Vienna, and on it is an inscription reading, “The probable site of his grave.”
pages.brief: After Mozart's death, his family is so poor they cannot purchase a gravestone, and eventually no one can remember where he was buried. Today a great monument to Mozart stands in Vienna at the probable site of his grave.

pages.text: Mozart’s music is still played today. He wrote such famous operas as The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute, and the piano piece, “Eine Kleine Nachtmusik” (which means “a little night music” in German). You may not have heard of these pieces of music, but if you heard them being played, you might recognize them. Mozart’s music is used everywhere. You can hear it in a concert hall, or you can hear it in cartoons. He wrote many of his most famous pieces when he was only a little older than you are. And he died while he was still young. Imagine the wealth of music we might have if he had only lived.
pages.brief: Mozart's music is still played today in concert halls and cartoons. People listen as his famous operas and piano piece are performed. He wrote many of his most famous pieces when he was only a little older than the reader, and he died while still young.

books.title: Día de los Muertos
books.art_why: The book shows real modern celebrations, people, parades, altars, and art that can be photographed today.

pages.text: United States Mexico.
pages.brief: A map of the United States and Mexico appears beside small scenes of a parade, an altar, sugar skulls, and children in costume. These images introduce the book’s topics about Día de los Muertos celebrations.

pages.text: Introduction Up ahead, skull puppets float in the air, and skeletons dance in the street, drummers march, and children wear masks and cardboard wings. You ask a woman with a painted face what’s happening. She tells you it’s a parade that honors friends and family who have died— it’s a Día de los Muertos parade.
pages.brief: In a lively street parade, skull puppets float overhead while skeletons dance and drummers march. Children wear masks and cardboard wings. A woman with a painted face speaks to a visitor, gesturing toward the parade that honors friends and family who have died.

pages.text: When and Where? People in many parts of the world celebrate Día de los Muertos, or “Day of the Dead.” People in Mexico have celebrated holidays like Día de los Muertos for thousands of years. All over the United States, people hold Day of the Dead parades and celebrations. These celebrations usually take place around November 1 and 2.
pages.brief: People in Mexico and the United States celebrate Día de los Muertos around November 1 and 2. Mexican families take part in long-held traditions, while U.S. communities hold parades and celebrations in decorated streets filled with people.

pages.text: Mexico Is It Halloween? Día de los Muertos might seem like Halloween, but the two holidays are different. Halloween is often about scaring people, but Día de los Muertos is a time of happiness and joy. Some people in certain cultures believe the spirits of loved ones come home to visit. People remember, honor, and celebrate those who have died.
pages.brief: A joyful Día de los Muertos scene contrasts with Halloween: instead of scary images, people smile among flowers and decorated skulls. Families remember, honor, and celebrate loved ones who have died, and some believe the spirits of loved ones come home to visit.

pages.text: In San Francisco, California, about 15,000 people carry candles and photos of loved ones who have died. Austin, Texas, has a large parade and costume contest to celebrate Day of the Dead. In Tucson (TOO- sawn), Arizona, more than 30,000 people march in a parade.
pages.brief: In San Francisco, California, about 15,000 people carry candles and photos of loved ones who have died. In Austin, Texas, a large parade and costume contest celebrate Day of the Dead. In Tucson, Arizona, more than 30,000 people march in a parade.

pages.text: Mexico Lidia’s Día de los Muertos Growing up in Mexico, Lidia Terán-Cooper celebrated Día de los Muertos. Lidia and her family spent every November 2 at the cemetery. The family brought flowers and a picnic, and they told stories about those who had died. Bands played special songs in honor of the dead. Lidia and the other children danced and played all day at the cemetery.
pages.brief: Lidia Terán-Cooper celebrates Día de los Muertos as a girl in Mexico. On November 2, her family gathers at the cemetery with flowers and a picnic. They tell stories about loved ones who died. Bands play special songs while Lidia and other children dance and play all day.

pages.text: Día de los Muertos was always a happy day for Lidia. She spent it remembering those she loved. Lidia lives in the United States now, but she and her family march in the parade in Tucson every year. Walking in the parade reminds her of celebrating Día de los Muertos when she was a little girl.
pages.brief: Lidia smiles as she remembers Día de los Muertos, a happy day spent remembering people she loved. Now living in the United States, she marches in the Tucson parade every year with her family. Walking in the parade brings back memories of celebrating as a little girl.

pages.text: In the days before the parade, Lidia makes masks. She shreds newspaper and soaks it in water, then she mixes the wet newspaper with flour and glue. Lidia turns the mixture into masks. When the masks are dry, children and adults paint them and wear them in the parade.
pages.brief: Before the parade, Lidia makes masks. She shreds newspaper, soaks it in water, and mixes the wet paper with flour and glue. She shapes the mixture into masks. When the masks dry, children and adults paint them and wear them in the parade.

pages.text: Day of the Dead for Children Some cities have a Day of the Dead celebration for children. Children decorate cardboard wings to wear in their special parade. They make loud noisemakers and learn tricks. They paint their faces and put on costumes.
pages.brief: In a Day of the Dead celebration for children, kids decorate cardboard wings to wear in their special parade. They make loud noisemakers and learn tricks. Children paint their faces and put on costumes for the lively event.

pages.text: Altars Día de los Muertos has many other traditions. Some people build altars in their homes to welcome the spirits of loved ones. The altars are covered with cloth and decorated with photos of the person who has died. They might include a favorite item or piece of clothing of the loved one.
pages.brief: Some families build altars in their homes to welcome the spirits of loved ones. The altars are covered with cloth and decorated with photos of the person who has died. A favorite item or piece of clothing of the loved one might be placed there.

pages.text: The family lights candles around the altars. They also make bread called pan de muertos, or “bread of the dead,” for the altars. A family may also leave a favorite juice or other drink. Orange and yellow marigolds or other flowers, skeleton toys, and dolls also decorate the altars. Do You Know? Some believe that marigolds help the spirits of loved ones find their way home, which is why they are often placed on altars. People will sometimes scatter marigold petals from their loved ones’ graves to the family’s front door.
pages.brief: Families light candles around altars and make pan de muertos, or bread of the dead. They may leave a favorite juice or drink. Orange and yellow marigolds, skeleton toys, and dolls decorate the altars. Some scatter marigold petals from graves to the family’s front door.

pages.text: Mexico Sugar Skulls and Art Some people who celebrate Día de los Muertos make sugar skulls. People decorate the sugar skulls with colorful frosting. Children in Mexico and the United States love eating the sweet skulls. Some artists paint colorful pictures in honor of Día de los Muertos. The paintings show skeletons dancing, playing music, and celebrating. The art is a way to celebrate friends and family members who have died.
pages.brief: People make sugar skulls and decorate them with colorful frosting. Children in Mexico and the United States love eating the sweet skulls. Some artists paint colorful pictures of skeletons dancing, playing music, and celebrating. The art celebrates friends and family members who have died.

pages.text: Full of Life Día de los Muertos helps people to feel better after losing someone they love. Marching in a parade or decorating altars can help them remember that special person. No other holiday is so full of fun, costumes, life, masks, joy, memories, and love.
pages.brief: A colorful Día de los Muertos scene shows people marching in a parade and decorating altars. The holiday helps people feel better after losing someone they love. Remembering that special person brings fun, costumes, life, masks, joy, memories, and love.

books.title: What Lives in This Hole?
books.art_why: Real animals, habitats, and maps are shown, so photographs fit the factual blog.

pages.text: From the deserts of Arizona to the streams and rivers of Japan, people have wondered What Lives in This Hole? Join the student author as he writes a class blog about burrowing animals from all over the world. Interesting photos and detailed maps give readers the opportunity.
pages.brief: A student author works on a class blog about burrowing animals. Around the scene are interesting photos of animals and detailed maps of deserts, streams, and rivers from Arizona to Japan. The focus is on curiosity about what lives inside a hole.

pages.text: My First Post! I found a large hole in the ground while hiking several months ago. I thought it was the opening to an animal’s burrow, although I had no idea what kind of animal lived there. I took a picture with my phone and asked my teacher if she knew.
pages.brief: A student hiker stands beside a large hole in the ground, holding a phone to take a picture. The hole looks like an animal’s burrow. The student wants to know what kind of animal lives there and plans to ask a teacher.

pages.text: My teacher taught me how to research to find the answer to my question and, before long, I started blogging! Every week, I research the burrow of one animal and post my work on our class blog. Some of my classmates have started blogging, too. You should check out my blog posts on the following pages!
pages.brief: A student works at a computer, writing a class blog about animal burrows. A teacher helps with research, and classmates sit nearby, also writing their own blog posts. The scene suggests a weekly routine of learning and sharing discoveries about one burrowing animal at a time.

pages.text: Utah Do You Know? California Desert tortoise burrows Arizona New can be up to 1.8 meters Mexico (6 ft) deep, but some are PACIFIC OCEAN only a little wider than the tortoise’s shell. MEXICO Staying Cool A desert tortoise lives in this hole! This reptile lives in deserts, and survives by digging a burrow to escape the blazing heat. The desert tortoise spends almost all of its life underground, sleeping there all winter to stay warm.
pages.brief: A desert tortoise stands at the entrance of its underground burrow in a hot desert. A simple map hints at the southwestern United States and Mexico, where the tortoise lives. The reptile uses the burrow to escape blazing heat and spends most of its life underground, sleeping there through winter.

pages.text: Wowser! The goliath spider is the in the world. Keeping Eggs Safe A spider the size of a dinner plate lives in this hole! The goliath bird-eating spider may dig its own deep burrow or use one that another animal no longer uses. A female stays in her burrow for most of her life. She lays around fifty eggs in a little silk egg sac, which she takes with her if she leaves to hunt.
pages.brief: A huge goliath bird-eating spider sits beside its deep burrow, its body as large as a dinner plate. The female holds a small silk egg sac containing around fifty eggs. If she leaves the burrow to hunt, she carries the egg sac with her.

pages.text: Making a Nest This hole belongs to Atlantic puffins! These birds use their strong wings and webbed feet to fly and swim. Puffins spend most of their life on the open ocean, so they swim much better than they fly.
pages.brief: An Atlantic puffin stands at the opening of its burrow on a cliff near the water. Its strong wings and webbed feet are visible, suited for both flying and swimming. The open ocean stretches behind the bird, showing where puffins spend most of their lives.

pages.text: Wowser! Adult Atlantic puffins have brightly colored bills during the breeding season. Puffins’ nicknames are “sea parrots” and “clowns of the sea.” Atlantic puffins raise their chicks in a burrow, which they dig on a cliff near water. They line the burrow with seaweed, plants, or feathers. Puffin parents take turns caring for a single egg until it hatches. Then one parent leaves to get small fish to feed the chick, while the other parent keeps the chick safe.
pages.brief: An adult Atlantic puffin with a brightly colored bill stands at a burrow dug into a cliff near water. Inside, the burrow is lined with seaweed, plants, and feathers. One parent carries small fish toward a single chick while the other parent stays close, keeping the chick safe.

pages.text: Wowser! The tunnels of one naked mole rat AFRICA AFRICA colony can cover as much land as twenty football fields! INDIAN INDIAN OCEAN OCEAN Living in the Dark Naked mole rats live in this hole! These small animals spend their entire lives underground in the dark. Small hairs on their face and tail help them find their way. They dig tunnels to find roots and other plant parts to eat.
pages.brief: Naked mole rats move through dark underground tunnels in Africa, their small face and tail hairs helping them find the way. The colony’s tunnels stretch as far as twenty football fields. Roots and other plant parts grow in the soil around them. A simple map hints at Africa and the Indian Ocean.

pages.text: Naked mole rats work as a team to build their tunnels. One animal breaks new soil at the front of the line. Behind it, several others use their feet to move dirt backward. A worker at the back kicks the dirt up to the surface. Different parts of the tunnels have different uses, such as food storage or nest areas.
pages.brief: A line of naked mole rats works as a team inside a tunnel. At the front, one breaks new soil; behind it, others use their feet to push dirt backward. A worker at the back kicks dirt up toward the surface. Side chambers are used for food storage and nest areas.

pages.text: Hiding and Laying Eggs A Japanese giant salamander lives in this underwater hole! This animal lives in cool mountain rivers and streams. During the day, it hides in a burrow or under rocks, and it comes out to hunt for food at night.
pages.brief: A Japanese giant salamander hides in an underwater burrow among rocks in a cool mountain stream. The large amphibian stays out of sight during the day. It rests among the rocky riverbed, waiting to come out and hunt at night.

pages.text: Wowser! Japanese giant salamanders are huge —they can grow as long as 1.5 meters (5 ft). In late summer, males and females gather at long burrows to breed. Females swim into the burrows to lay their eggs—they can have up to five hundred! A male watches the eggs to make sure fish don’t eat them.
pages.brief: A very large Japanese giant salamander male watches over a cluster of eggs inside a long underwater burrow. A female swims into the burrow after laying up to five hundred eggs. Nearby fish hover in the water, and the male stays close to keep the eggs safe.

pages.text: Wowser! A wombat’s burrow may be as long as three school buses! Staying Safe A wombat lives in this hole! This animal digs a burrow with its huge claws. Wombats stay in their burrows and sleep during the day, then come out at night to feed on plants. If an enemy chases them, they may run to their burrow or protect themselves by fighting.
pages.brief: A wombat with huge claws digs a long burrow that stretches as far as three school buses. The burrow entrance opens onto ground with plants nearby. Wombats sleep inside during the day and come out at night to feed, and they may run back to the burrow if an enemy chases them.

pages.text: Do You Know? Animals live in burrows on every continent—even Antarctica. More to Come So far, I’ve blogged about animal holes on six continents, so you might be wondering about Antarctica. I just learned that sea urchins live in burrows there, so check back soon for a post about them. I’m going to keep doing research on animals that live in holes because I really enjoy learning about the natural world!
pages.brief: A student author sits at a computer, writing a blog about animals that live in holes. A simple world map suggests six continents already covered, with Antarctica still to come. Nearby, a sea urchin rests inside a burrow under cold Antarctic water, ready for the next blog post.

books.title: Owls Overhead
books.art_why: Owls are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Owls may seem strange and mysterious, but that only makes them more fascinating. In Owls Overhead, students will learn about the different adaptations that allow these amazing predatory birds to survive in the wild.
pages.brief: An owl with large, forward-facing eyes and soft feathers perches on a branch, looking mysterious and alert. It is a predatory bird in the wild, shown as the subject of a book about its adaptations for survival.

pages.text: Flying in the Moonlight It’s a quiet, moonlit night, and you’re walking along the edge of town when a shadow suddenly crosses your path. You look up as a dark, silent shape glides over you and flies into the nearby trees.
pages.brief: On a quiet, moonlit night at the edge of town, a person walks along. A dark, silent shape glides overhead and flies into nearby trees; the person looks up as the shadow crosses the path.

pages.text: It’s an owl—one of more than two hundred different species of owls that live around the world. They come in many sizes and live on every continent except Antarctica. Owls may seem mysterious, but their appearance and actions help them survive.
pages.brief: Several owls of different sizes are shown together, representing more than two hundred species that live around the world on every continent except Antarctica. They may seem mysterious, and their appearance and actions help them survive in the wild.

pages.text: Eyes for the Night Like most birds, owls can’t move their eyes— instead, they must turn their heads to follow a moving object. Owls can turn their heads almost all the way around and even upside down, and they’re able to do this because they have twice as many neck bones as humans. Also, the blood vessels in their necks keep blood flowing in every body position.
pages.brief: An owl turns its head almost all the way around, even upside down, while its body stays still. It can do this because it has twice as many neck bones as humans, and blood vessels keep blood flowing in every position.

pages.text: Owls’ large eyes help them survive, too. Owls can’t see in total darkness, but they’re able to see better in low light than most animals. That’s because of their pupils—the black circles in the center of their eyes. Their pupils can grow large to allow more light to enter. When light is low, tawny owls see as much as one hundred times better than humans.
pages.brief: An owl in low light shows large eyes with big black pupils. The pupils grow large to let more light enter, and a tawny owl can see in dim conditions as much as one hundred times better than a human.

pages.text: Even Better Ears Most owls rely on their hearing to hunt. The majority of owls have huge ears, with one higher than the other. The higher ear hears sounds from above, while the lower ear hears sounds from below. Most owls have dish-shaped faces that collect sound waves and make the sounds louder. They move the feathers around their “dishes” to direct more sound to one ear or the other. Doing this helps them find prey.
pages.brief: An owl hunts by hearing, with huge ears one higher than the other and a dish-shaped face that collects sound waves. It moves the feathers around its face to direct more sound to one ear and find prey.

pages.brief: A great gray owl dives under snow to grab a hidden mouse, while a barn owl catches a mouse in complete darkness. Nearby, an owl coughs up a small pellet of fur, bone, teeth, and claws after swallowing prey whole.

pages.text: Silent Hunters Many animals that owls hunt also have very good hearing, so if an owl wants to eat them, it must attack by surprise. The soft feathers that cover owls’ bodies help them fly without a sound. Not all owls fly silently, however. For example, owls that hunt insects, which can’t hear well, don’t fly without a sound. Their feathers are slightly different from those of many other owls.
pages.brief: An owl flies without a sound, its body covered in soft feathers, and attacks prey by surprise because the animals it hunts have very good hearing. Another owl that hunts insects, which cannot hear well, has slightly different feathers and does not fly silently.

pages.text: All owls are meat eaters. Their main food is small animals—lots of them. A hungry great gray owl may eat 1,400 mice in a year. In its lifetime, a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice! In addition to small mammals, owls may eat frogs, snakes, lizards, birds, insects, and fish.
pages.brief: An owl, a meat eater, catches small animals. A hungry great gray owl may eat 1,400 mice in a year, and a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice in its lifetime. Owls may also eat frogs, snakes, lizards, birds, insects, and fish.

pages.text: Where Owls Live Some owls can live in many different habitats, but other owls need a special habitat. Burrowing owls live mostly on the prairie, making their nests underground and using old burrows dug by other animals. Sometimes they move into fields and golf courses, and even near airport runways. An Owl’s Housekeeper Screech owls hunt snakes, but they bring blindsnakes back to their nest alive and release them. These snakes eat the insects that feed on the dead animals stored there. In effect, blindsnakes become the owls’ housekeepers!
pages.brief: Burrowing owls on the prairie make nests underground in old burrows dug by other animals, and sometimes they move into fields, golf courses, or near airport runways. A screech owl brings a live blindsnake back to its nest, where the snake eats insects.

pages.text: Spotted owls can only survive in old forests with huge trees; they don’t do well in forests that grow back after being cut down. By 1994, most of their habitat had been destroyed by logging. Today, few spotted owls are left.
pages.brief: A spotted owl sits in an old forest with huge trees. It cannot do well in forests that grow back after being cut down; by 1994 logging had destroyed most of its habitat, and few spotted owls are left.

pages.text: Owl Sounds Owls aren’t always silent, and they don’t all hoot. Different owl species make different sounds. A great horned owl can bark like a dog and meow like a cat. Barn owls don’t hoot— they scream. Their strange cry and appearance once made some people think of barn owls as a sign of bad luck. Owls Are Out There People don’t often see owls, but they’re out there. If you’re in the country and want to find one, try going out at sunset and listening for their calls. Even in a city, you may spot an owl. They’re easiest to see in winter, when tree branches are bare.
pages.brief: A great horned owl barks like a dog and meows like a cat, while a barn owl screams instead of hooting; its strange cry and appearance once made people think of bad luck. At sunset in the country, or in a city in winter with bare branches, an owl may be spotted.

pages.text: If you stay out late enough, people might think you’re an owl—a night owl, that is.
pages.brief: A person stays out late at night under the night sky, and an owl is nearby. People might think the person is an owl—a night owl, that is—because they stay out so late.

books.title: Thurgood Marshall
books.art_why: A named famous person, Thurgood Marshall, so cartoon portraits fit.

pages.text: Having grown up in the segregated South of the United States, Thurgood Marshall spent his life working for equality. He helped to end school segregation in the United States and became a Supreme Court justice in 1967, among other accomplishments. Thurgood Marshall gives readers a glimpse into the legal mind and life’s work of a remarkable man. Thurgood Marshall was born in 1908 in Baltimore, Maryland. He was African American, and his grandfather had once been an enslaved person. Written by Marvin Bird.
pages.brief: A portrait of Thurgood Marshall as an adult Supreme Court justice in a black robe, standing beside a small scene of a baby in a Baltimore home with his parents and grandfather. The baby is wrapped in a blanket.

pages.text: By the time Thurgood was born, slavery was against the law. Even so, when Thurgood was a child, the South was still segregated. Black people were not allowed to eat in many restaurants that served white people.
pages.brief: A Black family stands outside a restaurant window, looking in at white customers eating at tables; a white server blocks the door with his hand raised. The family's child holds a parent's hand. The setting is a Southern street in the early 1900s.

pages.text: Black people were not allowed to sit in the same train cars as white people.
pages.brief: Inside a train, white passengers sit in one car, and Black passengers sit in a separate car behind a closed door. A Black child looks through the door's window at the white passengers. The train rolls through the Southern countryside.

pages.text: Black children in the South were not allowed to go to school with white children.
pages.brief: Two separate school buildings stand apart. White children walk into one school; Black children carry books toward the other, smaller school. A fence separates the two schoolyards. The Black children look toward the white school before turning away under a gray sky.

pages.text: Those laws were unfair. At the dinner table, Thurgood’s family used to argue about what to do about those laws. Thurgood became very good at arguing. Do You Know? Thurgood’s parents named him “Thoroughgood.” Because he didn’t like having to spell his name, he shortened it to Thurgood in second grade. His nickname was “Goody.”
pages.brief: Around a dinner table in a modest Baltimore home, young Thurgood Marshall argues with his hand raised, his mouth open. His mother and father listen, and his grandfather sits at the end. Plates and cups sit on the table. Thurgood looks confident and determined.

pages.text: After graduating from Lincoln University, an all-Black college, Marshall wanted to go to the University of Maryland Law School. Because he was Black, the school would not let him in. Instead, he went to the all-Black law school at Howard University. In 1933, he graduated first in his class and became a lawyer.
pages.brief: A young Thurgood Marshall in a graduation cap and gown stands at the front of a class of Black graduates at Howard University law school, holding his diploma. He smiles proudly. Behind him, a brick law school building and a row of classmates in caps and gowns.

pages.text: In 1936, he won his first big victory for civil rights. It was against the University of Maryland Law School—the same school he’d tried to attend. Another Black student was not allowed into the school because of his skin color. That student took the school to court, saying that keeping Black people out of the school was illegal. Marshall argued the case and won.
pages.brief: In a courtroom, Thurgood Marshall in a suit stands before a judge, pointing at a law book. Beside him sits a young Black student in a jacket. The University of Maryland Law School building appears in a small inset, with its doors closed to the student.

pages.text: Marshall went on to argue many cases before the Supreme Court —the most important court in the United States. Marshall argued a case about neighborhoods. He said that people of other races should be allowed to buy homes in white neighborhoods.
pages.brief: Thurgood Marshall stands at a podium before the nine Supreme Court justices in their robes, arguing a case. Below, a row of houses shows a Black family looking at a home for sale in a white neighborhood, white neighbors watching from porches.

pages.text: Marshall argued another case about segregation on buses and trains. He said that Black people and white people should be able to ride together. Marshall won these and many other cases for civil rights. In 1954, Marshall argued his most important case of all. In some states, Black children had to go to all-Black schools. Their parents thought this was wrong.
pages.brief: Marshall argues before the Supreme Court, one hand raised. Outside, a bus carries Black and white riders sitting together, and Black parents stand with their children outside an all-Black school, pointing toward the white school down the street.

pages.text: Marshall argued that it was unfair to have separate schools for Black children and white children. Separate schools were not equal, he argued. Instead, children of all races had to be able to attend the same public schools. Once again, Marshall won his case. Every justice on the Supreme Court voted to end segregation in public schools. The case inspired the civil rights movement and made Marshall famous.
pages.brief: Marshall stands outside the Supreme Court, smiling, as Black and white children walk together through the doors of one public school. Inside, the justices raise their hands in a unanimous vote. A crowd of parents cheers behind the children.

pages.text: In all, Marshall argued thirty-two cases before the Supreme Court and won twenty-nine of them. In 1965, he became the first Black lawyer to argue cases for the U.S. government before the Supreme Court. Two years later, the president chose Marshall to become the first Black justice on the Supreme Court.
pages.brief: Marshall in a suit argues before the Supreme Court; in another scene, the president shakes his hand in the White House. Then Marshall wears a black justice robe, standing before the Court as its first Black justice. He looks serious and proud.

Of the nine justices, there were no women and no people of color. Because the no women and no people of color. Because the president chooses each justice for life, it took president chooses each justice for life, it took a long time to make things more equal. The first a long time to make things more equal. The first change came when Thurgood Marshall became change came when Thurgood Marshall became a a justice in 1967. Then the first woman, Sandra justice in 1967. Then the first woman, Sandra Day Day O’Connor, joined the Court in 1981. In 2021, O’Connor, joined the Court in 1981. one African American man and three women were on the Court, including one Latina woman.
pages.brief: A group of nine white male Supreme Court justices sits in a row. Then Thurgood Marshall joins them in 1967, and Sandra Day O'Connor joins in 1981. By 2021, the Court includes one African American man and three women, including one Latina woman, seated together.

pages.text: Marshall still got to argue a lot, and he always argued to make things fair. He upheld the rights of children, women, homeless people, and people in prison. Marshall served on the Supreme Court for twenty-four years. In 1991, he retired. At that time, reporters asked him if Black people were better off than when he’d joined the court. “All Americans are better off since I joined the Court,” Marshall said. “All of them.” He died two years later. Marshall was a powerful voice for civil rights and a hero to everyone who believed in equality.
pages.brief: Marshall, older now, speaks to a crowd of reporters at a press conference, one hand raised. Behind him stand a child, a woman, a homeless person, and a prisoner, all listening. Marshall smiles warmly as he answers questions.

books.title: Wiggly Worms
books.art_why: Earthworms are real animals that can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Most people don’t think much about the small and slimy earthworm, but worms actually have a big role in our environment. Wiggly Worms teaches students about a worm’s body and behaviors, how it helps plants and other animals, and its place in the food chain.
pages.brief: A small, slimy earthworm curls through dark soil among plant roots, with a few other small animals nearby, showing how a creature that most people ignore plays a big role in the environment and the food chain.

pages.text: Small Animals, Big Changes Can you guess what animal eats dirt, builds tunnels in the soil, and emerges from the ground at night? If you guessed an earthworm, you’re right! Earthworms, or night crawlers, are found all around the world. These small animals affect the soil in big ways.
pages.brief: An earthworm emerges from damp soil at night, its body stretched out. Around it are patches of soil and low plants, showing a small animal found all around the world that affects the soil in big ways.

pages.text: Earthworm Bodies An earthworm’s body is shaped like one tube wrapped around the outside of another tube. A tube of muscle surrounds a tube that digests, or breaks down, the food that the worm eats. An earthworm’s body has more than one hundred ring-shaped parts, each of which can bend and stretch when the worm moves.
pages.brief: A close-up of an earthworm’s body shows many ring-shaped parts bending and stretching as the worm moves. A simple cutaway view reveals an inner tube for digesting food surrounded by an outer tube of muscle.

pages.text: An earthworm moves by extending, or stretching out, and contracting, or pulling in, its body parts. Small bristles on the worm’s body help it grip the ground. Earthworm Facts Common names Earthworm, night crawler Classification Invertebrate (no backbone) Life span Up to 6 years Size (common species) 3½–12 inches (9–30 cm) Habitat All types except deserts and areas where the ground is always frozen; prefer moist, rich soil.
pages.brief: An earthworm moves across damp, moist, rich soil, stretching its front end forward and pulling its back end in as it travels. Tiny bristles along its body touch the ground to help it grip firmly.

pages.text: Slimy Worms! Slimy mucus on an earthworm’s skin helps it to stay cool and wet and to slide through soil. When they dig tunnels, earthworms leave a mucus trail behind them that hardens on the tunnel walls, preventing them from collapsing.
pages.brief: Inside a long underground tunnel, an earthworm slides through damp soil. Its skin looks wet and shiny with slimy mucus, and a slick mucus trail hardens along the tunnel walls, keeping the walls from collapsing.

pages.text: Worms also use mucus to protect their eggs after they mate. The mucus hardens into a worm cocoon where baby worms can stay for weeks or months. The young worms emerge from the cocoon when the soil is warm and wet enough for them to survive. How do earthworms breathe? Earthworms don’t breathe through their mouths. Instead, they breathe through their skin, absorbing oxygen directly from the air. That’s why earthworms crowd sidewalks when the soil is full of rain: underwater, they will drown. They can’t survive if their skin dries out, either, because they can only breathe when their skin is moist.
pages.brief: A mucus cocoon lies in warm, wet soil with tiny young earthworms emerging. Nearby, earthworms crowd a wet sidewalk after rain, their moist skin absorbing oxygen, showing why they cannot stay underwater or dry out.

pages.text: Earthworm Behavior Earthworms construct long tunnels underground. The tunnels protect worms from heat and sunlight, and they help earthworms hide from hungry animals. If a bird attacks, an earthworm can escape by retreating into its tunnel.
pages.brief: An earthworm retreats into a long underground tunnel it has constructed, away from bright sunlight and heat. Above the soil, a hungry bird waits, but the tunnel gives the worm a hiding place and an escape route.

pages.text: Earthworms don’t have ears, but they can sense tiny movements in the ground. They don’t have eyes, but they have special parts of their skin that can sense light. Earthworms avoid bright light. Earthworms are night crawlers because they emerge at night in search of food. They use their mouths to pull dead leaves and plants into their tunnels to eat later.
pages.brief: At night, an earthworm emerges from its tunnel and uses its mouth to pull a dead leaf into the soil. It has no ears or eyes, but its skin senses light and tiny movements in the ground.

pages.text: Earthworms Are Good for the Soil Farmers love earthworms! When earthworms construct tunnels, they create space in the soil, and the space helps plants get the air and water they require to grow. Earthworms also put organic matter, such as rotting leaves, into the soil. Organic matter acts like a sponge to soak up water, so soil stays wet longer.
pages.brief: In a farm garden, an earthworm tunnels through soil beside plant roots. Its tunnels leave spaces that let air and water reach the plants, while rotting leaves mixed into the soil soak up water like a sponge.

pages.text: Earthworms also put nutrients into the soil that come from their waste, or castings. Castings make excellent fertilizer. In a garden smaller than the average classroom, earthworms can make 170 pounds (77 kg) of castings every year. That’s like fifteen bowling balls’ worth of worm waste!
pages.brief: Earthworm castings, dark and rich, are mixed into garden soil around healthy plants. A small garden scene suggests the amount: heaps of castings comparable to fifteen bowling balls’ worth of worm waste in a year.

pages.text: Some people raise earthworms on worm farms. They feed the earthworms food scraps, which the worms then transform into rich soil. Both earthworms and their castings can be sold to gardeners to improve their soil. Earthworms are also sold for fishing bait.
pages.brief: On a worm farm, people place food scraps into bins of soil where earthworms turn the scraps into rich castings. Nearby, bags of worms and castings are ready for gardeners, and some worms are set aside for fishing bait.

pages.text: Wanted: Earthworms! Farmers aren’t the only ones who are fans of earthworms. Moles, rats, and toads love juicy night crawlers. That’s because they enjoy eating them! Fish think earthworms are tasty, too. Earthworms are an important food source for these and other animals.
pages.brief: A mole, a rat, and a toad gather near damp soil where juicy night crawlers move, and a fish waits in nearby water. These animals see earthworms as tasty food, making the worms an important food source.

pages.text: Earthworms may be small, but they have a big job: helping plants grow! In one night, an earthworm can... • Eat up to one-third of its body weight • Travel up to 60 feet (18 m)—the distance from the pitcher’s mound to home plate in a baseball diamond.
pages.brief: An earthworm moves through soil beside growing plants, showing its big job in a small body. In one night it can eat up to one-third of its body weight and travel up to 60 feet, the distance from a baseball pitcher’s mound to home plate.

books.art_why: The book shows real animals and the real structures they build.

pages.brief: Sociable weaver birds crowd together around a huge nest made of large sticks and dry grass, with many entrances and a roof. Inside, softer grasses line rooms for sleeping and eating, and family groups come and go.

pages.text: Welcome to Tunnel Town Prairie Dog Towns A maze of prairie dog tunnels is like a real town. The.
pages.brief: A maze of prairie dog tunnels stretches through the ground like a real town. Prairie dogs stand near the tunnels and move between connected passages, and the many tunnels create a town-like network for them underground.

pages.text: Termite Mounds Tiny termites can build mounds that are taller than three people standing on top of each other! They build their mounds with mud and chewed wood. The walls have tiny holes for fresh air. One Queen, 165 Million Eggs! The king and queen termite live in a special room. The queen can produce thousands of eggs per day and can live up to age forty-five. Worker termites carry her young to a nursery room where they are fed until they are adults.
pages.brief: Tiny termites build a mound taller than three people standing on top of each other, using mud and chewed wood. Tiny holes in the walls let in fresh air. Inside, the king and queen sit in a special room while workers carry the young to a nursery.

pages.text: Pufferfish Circles These male fish make sand art to attract females. They form a large round pattern on the seafloor and decorate the circle with shells. If a female likes the circle, she lays her eggs in the middle.
pages.brief: A male pufferfish makes a large round sand pattern on the seafloor to attract a female. He decorates the circle with shells. A female pufferfish approaches, and if she likes the circle, she lays her eggs in the middle.

pages.text: Spider Trapdoors These sly spiders dig an underground tunnel and make a trapdoor on top. They cover the trapdoor with their silk, and then cover that with dirt. When prey passes above them, they open the door and the prey falls through.
pages.brief: A spider has dug an underground tunnel and made a trapdoor on top. It covers the trapdoor with silk and then dirt. When prey passes above, the spider opens the door, and the prey falls through into the tunnel.

pages.text: Underground Ant City Millions of ants work together to build underground ant cities. These giant cities have dirt “highways” that connect rooms. Side roads lead to gardens and trash pits.
pages.brief: Millions of ants work together to build an underground city. Dirt highways connect the rooms, and side roads lead to gardens and trash pits. The ants are shown moving through the tunnels and rooms of their giant city.

pages.text: Little Ants, Big City Researchers found a huge, empty underground city in Brazil, once the home of leafcutter ants. In order to build their home, each insect would have carried loads of earth more than half a mile (0.8 km)—over and over. In total, the ants moved around 45 tons (40 mt) of soil to create their network of tunnels. Ants at Work.
pages.brief: A huge, empty underground city in Brazil is shown, once the home of leafcutter ants. Researchers found the network of tunnels. Each ant would have carried loads of earth more than half a mile, over and over, moving about 45 tons of soil in total.

pages.text: Paper Wasp Nests Paper wasps chew bits of wood and plants to make a soft nest. The nest is made up of cells that look like an egg carton. Wasp eggs grow in the cells. As the wasps grow in number, the nest gets bigger.
pages.brief: Paper wasps chew bits of wood and plants to make a soft nest. The nest has cells that look like an egg carton, and wasp eggs grow inside them. As the wasps grow in number, the nest grows bigger.

pages.text: Crayfish Chimneys Crayfish dig into moist soil to reach water. The dirt they push up looks like a small chimney. Other animals, such as snakes, sometimes hide in the empty chimney.
pages.brief: A crayfish digs into moist soil to reach water, pushing up dirt that looks like a small chimney. A snake sometimes hides in an empty chimney. The crayfish and its chimney are shown near wet soil.

pages.text: Beaver Dams and Dens Busy beavers use sticks and mud to build their dams. The dams make ponds. Beavers build their homes, called dens, in the ponds. The ponds protect the beavers from other animals. The Best of Both Worlds.
pages.brief: Busy beavers use sticks and mud to build a dam. The dam makes a pond, and the beavers build their homes, called dens, in the pond. The pond protects the beavers from other animals, and the beavers are shown working together.

pages.text: Caddisfly Cocoons These little insects use their silk to make add sand, small shells to their cocoons to make cases. Watch Them Build Animals build great things. They do not need tools to build. They just use their bodies and the Earth around them. Animals are amazing!
pages.brief: Small caddisfly insects use silk to make cocoons and add sand and small shells to their cases. Other animals build great things too, using their bodies and the Earth around them without tools. The animals are shown with their built homes and cases.

books.title: The Amazing Amazon
books.art_why: The Amazon rainforest, its animals, river, and people are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Chapter 1: There Is a Place There is a place where monkeys swing and howl. There is a place where jaguars leap from tree to tree. Bananas and pineapples grow for free. Tiny frogs live in flowers. Pink-colored dolphins swim in the river. Storms come often. The air is sweet. A little sunlight filters through the vines and leaves, but it is mostly dark on the ground. It is hot, steamy, and still. Rainwater flows from leaf to leaf. You are sweating. A bug lands on your neck. An ant quietly walks across your shoe. Suddenly a little brown monkey swings to a nearby branch. Then a bright green bird flies past. Welcome to the Amazon rainforest.
pages.brief: A hot, steamy Amazon rainforest with vines and leaves filtering little sunlight onto a dark floor. Monkeys swing and howl while a jaguar leaps between trees. Bananas and pineapples grow, a tiny frog sits in a flower, and pink dolphins swim in the river. A sweating visitor feels a bug on the neck and an ant on the shoe.

pages.text: Rainforests Tropical rainforests are forests where it rains a lot. In fact, a tropical rainforest receives between 150 and 400 centimeters (59–157 in) of rain every year. They are also warm. The ranges temperature from 25° to 35° Celsius (77°F–95°F). Rainforests are green year-round. Their hot and humid climate is perfect for tall trees and other plants. The really thick parts of rainforests are what we call jungles. Tropical rainforests cover a small part (about 6 percent) of Earth’s surface. But more than half (50 percent) of the world’s plant and animal species are found in them! Rainforests are usually near Earth’s equator. Most of the world’s rainforests are in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America.
pages.brief: A warm, humid tropical rainforest under heavy rain, with tall green trees and thick plants that stay green all year. A wide view of Earth shows rainforest regions near the equator in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America. Rain falls often, and the hot, steamy air surrounds the dense forest.

pages.text: The Amazon The Amazon rainforest is in South America. It is the largest tropical rainforest in the world. It has more kinds of insects, plants, and animals than any other place on Earth. Every year, scientists discover new species of insects and plants here. The Amazon River flows through the heart of this rainforest. Thousands of other rivers and streams empty into it. Many fish and other animals live in the Amazon River. This book will take you through the Amazon rainforest. You will travel from the tallest trees to the rainforest floor. Along the way, you will meet an eagle, monkey, jaguar, and ant. You will even hear what they would say—if they could talk.
pages.brief: A broad view of the Amazon rainforest in South America, with the wide Amazon River flowing through the heart of dense green trees and many streams emptying into it. Scientists study new insects and plants. An eagle, a monkey, a jaguar, and an ant appear among the trees, from the tallest trees down to the forest floor.

pages.text: Map of Amazon Basin ATLANTIC OCEAN So just how big is the Amazon River? • The Amazon River can be more than 48 kilometers (30 mi) across at its widest point during the rainy season. • It flows almost 6,437 kilometers (4,000 mi) to the Atlantic Ocean. • The river’s arapaima fish can grow to be 3 meters (10 ft) long and weigh 180 kilograms (400 lb)! • Its volume is greater than the next eight largest rivers combined!
pages.brief: A wide map-like view of the Amazon Basin, with the Amazon River crossing South America and reaching the Atlantic Ocean. The river stretches very wide during the rainy season. A long arapaima fish swims in the water, and the river's great volume is suggested by many connected waterways.

pages.text: From the Amazon Yearbook Sloths are slow- moving animals. They seem to just hang out (upside down!) in the trees. The tapir is a big, hoofed animal that is related to the horse and the rhinoceros. Tapirs often weigh well over 136 kilograms (300 lb). At around 1.2 meters (4 ft) long, the capybara is the world’s largest rodent. (But don’t call Katie a big rat.) The poison arrow frog has super-bright colors. These colors warn other animals that its skin is poisonous.
pages.brief: A rainforest yearbook scene with a sloth hanging upside down in a tree, a big hoofed tapir standing nearby, and a capybara beside water. A poison arrow frog shows its super-bright colors on the forest floor. The animals rest among leaves and branches, each one shown clearly in its rainforest home.

pages.text: Chapter 2: Layers of the Rainforest To better understand the rainforest, scientists have “divided” it into four parts. You can think of it like a four-story building. The highest trees make up the top floor, or the emergent layer. The next highest trees make up the canopy layer. Below them is the understory. At the bottom is the rainforest floor. Rainforest Layers High Risers The tallest trees of the rainforest are called the emergents. They are like umbrellas that rise above the thick forest. Emergents receive lots of sun, wind, and rain. Big roots support these giant trees. Because the soil isn’t deep, tree roots often grow above the ground. The kapok tree, for example, has roots that extend out like wooden walls. These roots are so big that your whole class could hide behind just one of them! Not many animals live in the emergent layer. Some birds and butterflies eat the leaves and fruit. One huge bird, the harpy eagle, actually lives there, high above the river.
pages.brief: A tall rainforest shown in four levels like a four-story building: the highest emergent trees, the canopy, the understory, and the dark floor. Giant kapok roots spread out above the ground like wooden walls. A harpy eagle perches high above a river.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Harpy Eagle Interviewer: Hello there, Harpy. Is it true that you are the largest eagle in the Americas? Harpy: I think so. I am about one meter tall, which is more than three feet high. Interviewer: It looks as if you have some big wings as well. Harpy: Oh, these things? I was born with these. If I stretch them out like this, they are longer than most people. You see? My wingspan is two meters across—about six and a half feet. Flying fast really helps me find food. Interviewer: What is your favorite food? Harpy: Oh, I like pizza delivered to my door. Just kidding—I hunt sloths, monkeys, and other birds. Monkeys are probably my favorite. Interviewer: Is that what your big talons are for? Harpy: Yep. They can scoop unsuspecting animals right off tree branches. Hey, there’s a monkey now! I’ll see you later!
pages.brief: A large harpy eagle stands on a high branch, stretching its wide wings for a small interviewer holding a microphone. The eagle's big talons grip the wood. A monkey appears on a nearby branch. The interviewer looks up, listening to the eagle.

pages.text: Crazy Canopy The rainforest’s real action is in the canopy layer. This is where most plants and animals live. It is like a thick roof made out of tree branches and vines. Many trees in the canopy are covered with climbing vines and epiphytes. Epiphytes are plants that grow on top of other plants. Most of the rainforest’s flowers, fruit, and seeds are found in this layer. With so much good canopy food, it makes sense that animals hang out here. Many animals rarely go down to the ground. They spend their whole lives up in the trees. Sloths, toucans, and parrots are just some of the animals that live in the canopy. Howler monkeys are probably the loudest. Their name fits their behavior, as these monkeys howl and scream to keep other animals out of their territories. Bromeliads are cone- shaped plants that grow on trees. Their cones catch a lot of rainwater and form little swimming pools high above the ground. Tiny frogs, salamanders, and crabs live in these pools. Mosquitoes and dragonflies lay eggs in them.
pages.brief: High in the thick canopy, branches and vines form a leafy roof. A sloth hangs upside down while toucans, parrots, and howler monkeys move among flowers and fruit. Cone-shaped bromeliads hold small pools of rainwater, where tiny frogs, salamanders, and crabs rest and dragonflies hover.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Howler Monkey Interviewer: Wow, that was one loud howl! Would you please stop screaming for one moment? I would like to ask you a few questions! Howler: Okay, but hurry up. If I don’t scream like this, other monkeys may come into our territory. Interviewer: Do you always stay up here in the canopy? Howler: This is our home, my man. On the ground, there are some really big animals— it’s a jungle down there. Up here, we can eat fruit, leaves, and flowers, and we can live in safety. Interviewer: Does your long tail help you? It looks prehensile. Howler: Yeah, if by prehensile you mean “grab onto.” My tail helps me climb, but my hands and feet are very useful for climbing, too. Interviewer: You sure use big words for a monkey. Hey, stop the howling! If you can be heard from miles away, just think how loud it is for me. What makes you so loud anyway? Howler: I have a special bone in my windpipe. My throat is like a hollow sound box. Interviewer: Okay, Mr. Monkey, you can go back to howling now.
pages.brief: In the canopy, a howler monkey opens its mouth in a loud howl while an interviewer covers their ears and holds a microphone. The monkey's long tail curls around a branch. Fruit, leaves, and flowers surround them. Other monkeys stay away in nearby trees.

pages.text: The Darker Story The understory is the third level of the rainforest. It is below the canopy and above the ground. This is where ferns, plants, and young trees grow. It is dark in the understory because very little light shines through the thick canopy. Understory plants grow leaves that are big and wide to catch more sun. Animals like to eat these big leaves. The understory is not nearly as busy as the canopy, but animals do live here. Poison arrow frogs hide in the leaves. Snakes wrap around trees like vines. Birds eat insects from the wood. Large cats such as jaguars leap between branches.
pages.brief: In the dark understory beneath the canopy, ferns, young trees, and plants with big wide leaves grow. A bright poison arrow frog hides among leaves. A snake wraps around a tree trunk, a bird pecks insects from wood, and a jaguar leaps between branches.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Jaguar Interviewer: Hey, put me down! And don’t bite. Bad big cat! Jaguar: Sorry, I thought you were a monkey. What are you doing here anyway? Interviewer: I came to talk to you, the biggest cat in the Americas. Mr. Jaguar, are you really 2.6 meters (8.5 ft.) long? Jaguar: That’s what they say. I weigh 136 kilograms (300 lb), too. Not many animals mess with me. You can call me Jag. Interviewer: Okay, Jag, what do you do for exercise? Jag: I get bored with just one sport. That’s why I cross-train: I run, swim, climb, and fish when I hunt. Interviewer: What do you hunt? Jag: Sometimes I climb up in the canopy to eat sloths and monkeys. On the ground, I hunt peccaries, tapirs, and yummy capybaras. On lazy days, I lie near the river and catch fish. When I’m really hungry, I kill caimans. Interviewer: Wow, I don’t want to be in your powerful jaws ever again! Excuse me, I need to go now.
pages.brief: A powerful jaguar stands beside the river with an interviewer close by, the big cat's jaws near the interviewer. Around them are trees and water; a caiman lurks, a capybara moves on the bank, and a monkey and sloth are up in the canopy.

pages.text: Chapter 3: Keeping It Clean If you walked around the rainforest floor, you might be surprised. It is not just one thick jungle. Sure, you would see roots, plants, and baby trees. But most of the green would be high above you. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria eat up the fallen fruits and parts of trees. They recycle it back into nutritious soil. When a big tree falls, they munch it down into small pieces. Also on the ground are animals like deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras. But there are far more spiders and bugs. Ant highways crisscross the rainforest floor. One kind of ant even parades around with leaves and flower petals in its mouth. It is the famous leaf-cutter ant. Reaching the Top Scientists have found creative ways to study the top layers of rainforests. They have climbed with ropes and ladders. They have built platforms like tree houses. Some have gone up in cranes. A blimp has even lowered a raft of scientists down to the canopy.
pages.brief: On the rainforest floor, roots, plants, and baby trees surround fallen fruit. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria break down a fallen tree. A deer, tapir, peccary, and capybara stand nearby while spiders and leaf-cutter ants carry leaves along trails. Above, scientists use ropes, ladders, platforms, a crane, and a blimp to reach the canopy.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Leaf-Cutter Ant Interviewer: Hey down there! The one carrying the big leaf over your head! May I ask you a few questions? Ms. Ant: Sure, but I do need to hurry back to the fungus garden. We’re low on food. Interviewer: Did you really just climb up a tree and cut off that leaf? Ms. Ant: Yes, and now I’m carrying it back to our underground home. That’s where smaller ants will chew it up into spongy bits. Interviewer: So you don’t eat the leaf? Ms. Ant: No, we use the leaf bits to grow the fungus that we eat. Want some? Interviewer: No, thank you. I just had lunch. So tell me, what is it like underground? Ms. Ant: We have deep nests with lots of rooms. In the middle rooms, small ants tend to our fungus gardens. Our queen is in a different room. She can lay up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. That’s why there are almost five million of us here! Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to sniff my way home. And please watch your feet—if you step on our trail, I might get lost!
pages.brief: A small interviewer kneels on the forest floor, speaking to a leaf-cutter ant carrying a big leaf over its head. Behind them, a line of ants marches along a trail toward an underground nest with many rooms, where fungus gardens grow and a queen lays eggs.

pages.text: Chapter 4: Who, Me? Yes, you. Do you like to eat bananas or chocolate? Does your bicycle have rubber tires? Well, guess what! Bananas, chocolate, and rubber all grow in the Amazon rainforest. Many more things come from the Amazon, too, such as medicines and pineapples. The Amazon is a treasure. Insects buzz by that haven’t been named yet. Trees grow, fall, and turn back into soil. And rainforest plants take carbon dioxide from the air and replace it with oxygen. Humans and other animals need oxygen in order to live. The Amazon rainforest is a real place. As you read these words, a jaguar moves through the understory. Right now, a leaf-cutter ant marches back to a fungus garden. Somewhere in the Amazon, the scream of a howler monkey echoes through the forest. Can you hear it?
pages.brief: A child holds a banana and a piece of chocolate near bicycle tires, with pineapples and rubber trees around. In the rainforest, unnamed insects buzz, a jaguar moves through the understory, a leaf-cutter ant marches home, and a howler monkey's scream echoes through the trees.

pages.text: Explore More Did you like learning about the Amazon rainforest? Well, there is much more to see. If you do some research, you’re bound to find some very interesting animals! 1. At the Library Tell your librarian that you are interested in books about the Amazon rainforest. 2. On the Web In the address window, type: www.google.com Then type: Amazon rainforest. Click on “Google Search.” Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. When you want to explore other links, click the “back” arrow on the top left. Or try a new search: Amazon River.
pages.brief: A young reader stands in a library with a librarian, looking at books about the Amazon rainforest. Nearby, a computer screen shows a search page with colored links. The reader points to an interesting link, ready to explore more about the Amazon River.

pages.text: 3. Try This! Where do you live? Do you live in the rainforest? What about in a desert, tundra, or pine forest? Do you live on the coast, up in the mountains, or out on the plains? You must live somewhere, right? If you live in a town or city, sometimes it can be hard to tell what kind of region you live in. But there are clues all around. What kinds of trees and bushes grow nearby? What kinds of birds fly overhead? What is the weather like? Look around and investigate. If you are not sure, ask your teacher, librarian, parent, or friend. Once you figure it out, make a report. Draw a picture like the one on page 9, but make it for your area. What kind of insects, plants, and animals are native to your home? You could find this information by walking around outside. You could also ask other people.
