Or you could read a book or search the Web. You’ll probably be surprised by the cool things you learn about your neighbors!
pages.brief: A child stands outside a town or city, looking at nearby trees, bushes, and birds under the sky. On a table, the child makes a report with a drawing of local insects, plants, and animals. A teacher, librarian, parent, and friend stand nearby, ready to help answer questions.

books.title: Strange Plants
books.art_why: The book shows real plants that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Some plants eat meat. Some even steal food from other plants. In Strange Plants, readers will learn about several extraordinary plants. Detailed photographs accompany the engaging text. When we think about plants, we often think of trees, flowers, bushes, and grass. Most plants, like the ones in this photograph, Written by Kira Freed have roots growing into the ground as well as stems, green leaves, and sometimes flowers.
pages.brief: A close view of an ordinary green plant growing in soil, with roots reaching down into the ground, stems rising up, green leaves, and a flower. This example shows the basic parts common to many plants, like trees, bushes, and grass.

pages.text: While most plants have these four basic parts, some plants are different. This book explores what makes some of these strange plants unusual.
pages.brief: Several different plants are shown close together, each with unusual shapes or growth habits rather than the four basic parts described for most plants. The view invites readers to compare these plants and see what makes them different.

pages.text: Plants commonly called air plants live in trees high above the ground near ponds, streams, rivers, and swamps in North and South America. These plants don’t live in soil as most plants do—they live on tree branches! Instead of getting water from the soil through their roots, they get moisture from the air through their leaves. They only use their roots to hold tight to branches.
pages.brief: Air plants cling to tree branches high above the ground near a pond, stream, river, or swamp. Their leaves take moisture from the air, while their roots hold tightly to the branch instead of growing in soil.

pages.text: Unbelievable though it may seem, plants exist that eat meat. They eat insects, spiders, and even some fish, amphibians, reptiles, and small mammals. Like all plants, they use sunlight and water to produce their own food. However, the soil they grow in doesn’t provide them with everything they need to be healthy. The animals they “eat” on the side help them grow better.
pages.brief: A meat-eating plant is shown with insects, spiders, or small animals nearby in its moist growing place. It still uses sunlight and water to make food, but the animals it catches help it grow better because its soil lacks something it needs.

pages.text: One well-known meat-eating, or carnivorous, plant is the Venus flytrap. This plant lives in moist environments. Its leaves look like traps with small spikes along the edges and special hairs on the inside. When a critter walks inside a leaf and brushes against the hairs, the leaf snaps shut. The critter is trapped by the spikes.
pages.brief: A Venus flytrap grows in a moist environment, its leaves open like traps with small spikes along the edges and special hairs inside. A small critter walks inside a leaf and brushes the hairs, and the leaf snaps shut, trapping the critter behind the spikes.

pages.text: The sundew, another carnivorous plant that lives in moist environments, catches its food in a different way. Sticky hairs on its surface smell sweet. Insects attracted to the smell land and get stuck. Then the plant digests the insects. The giant sundew plant of Australia even eats small frogs!
pages.brief: A sundew plant grows in a moist place, its surface covered with sticky hairs that smell sweet. An insect lands on the hairs and becomes stuck. The plant then digests the insect; a giant sundew in Australia can even catch small frogs.

pages.text: Some plants steal food from other plants. The dodder plant lives on many continents but is most common in North and South America. It sends slender rootlike stems into another plant and sucks food and water from the plant. The dodder plant is a parasite —a living thing that lives off another living thing. When a dodder plant attaches to a plant to feed, its connection to the soil dies.
pages.brief: A dodder plant sends slender, rootlike stems into another plant, taking food and water from it. The dodder is a parasite living off the other plant. Once it attaches and feeds, its own connection to the soil dies.

pages.text: Many flowers have bad smells that attract insects. The stapelia flower, also called the “carrion flower,” smells like rotting meat. On hot days, the odor is noticeable from about 1.6 kilometers (1 mi.) away. The flower has a pattern that looks like dead animals. Flies are attracted to the pattern as well as the smell, so they fly into the flower. Special powder called “pollen” gets on their bodies, and they carry it to other flowers. The flowers use the powder to make seeds and grow new plants.
pages.brief: A stapelia flower, also called a carrion flower, opens with a pattern that looks like dead animals. Flies are drawn to its rotting-meat smell and the pattern, landing on the flower. Pollen gets on their bodies, and they carry it to other flowers so seeds can grow.

pages.text: Some plants look like stones. The plants in this photograph are called “stone plants” or “living stones.” They live in very hot, dry places such as South Africa. They hold water very well because the biggest part of each plant lives underground. These plants are tiny and usually have only two leaves. Their shape helps them hide so animals don’t eat them.
pages.brief: Tiny stone plants, or living stones, grow in a very hot, dry place such as South Africa. Most of each plant lives underground and holds water well. Usually only two leaves show above the ground, and their shape helps them hide from animals.

pages.text: Some cactus plants are covered with wool- like hairs. These plants come from Bolivia and Peru, high in the Andes Mountains of South America. The “wool” protects them from daytime heat and nighttime cold. It also helps the cactus plants hold moisture.
pages.brief: A cactus covered with wool-like hairs grows high in the Andes Mountains of South America, in Bolivia and Peru. The wool protects it from daytime heat and nighttime cold and helps the cactus hold moisture in its harsh mountain home.

pages.text: Some trees and shrubs grow out of solid rock. They grow up high where the wind blows strong. The wind can blow seeds into small cracks in the rock. When rain gets into the cracks, the seeds start to grow. Their roots reach down into small cracks for moisture. As the roots continue to grow, they split the rock.
pages.brief: A tree or shrub grows out of a crack in solid rock, high where the wind blows strong. Wind-blown seeds landed in the crack, rain helped them start growing, and roots reach down for moisture, splitting the rock as they grow.

pages.text: Some plants have animals living inside them. Ant colonies live inside ant plants. The ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it. They use spaces in the plant’s stem as houses. Some spaces are used for raising young ants, while other spaces are used for garbage. The ant plant uses some of this garbage for food.
pages.brief: An ant plant holds an ant colony inside spaces in its stem. Some spaces are used as houses for raising young ants, while others hold garbage. The ants protect the plant from animals that would eat it, and the plant uses some garbage for food.

pages.text: Many more kinds of strange plants also exist. Bamboo makes noise when it grows, and some Australian orchids grow and flower completely underground. Bat plants have fruit that looks like bats hanging upside down from the flowers. Some ghost plants have white flowers that seem to appear out of nowhere. There are many amazing plants in the world.
pages.brief: Several strange plants are shown: bamboo that makes noise as it grows, Australian orchids that grow and flower underground, bat plants with fruit looking like hanging bats, and ghost plants with white flowers that seem to appear from nowhere.

books.title: Sugar, Sugar, Everywhere
books.art_why: Real foods, factories, drinks, and body-health scenes are shown as they exist today.

pages.text: Many people love sugary desserts, but do they know that sugar also exists in other common foods such as ketchup and yogurt? Sugar, Sugar, Everywhere introduces readers to the important role of glucose in the body. Students will also learn how sugar is added to many foods, and how too much added sugar can be unhealthy for the body.
pages.brief: On a kitchen table, an inviting dessert sits beside a ketchup bottle, a yogurt cup, and fresh fruit, showing that sugar appears in many common foods. A person's hand reaches toward the dessert while the other foods remain in clear view.

pages.text: Introduction Which ingredient makes desserts and treats taste sweet? It’s sugar! You might be surprised to learn that desserts and treats are not the only foods that have sugar in them. In fact, people add sugar to many foods you wouldn’t expect.
pages.brief: A cook in a bright kitchen sprinkles sugar over a bowl of dessert, with several sweet treats arranged nearby. The scene suggests that sugar is the ingredient making desserts taste sweet, and that it can be added to foods in everyday cooking.

pages.text: What Is Sugar? Sugar is a natural part of plant foods and milk. Apples, pears, and grapes are full of natural sugar. Many vegetables contain sugar and starch, which breaks down into sugar. The white crystals in a sugar bowl are table sugar, which is different from the sugar found in fruits and vegetables.
pages.brief: A wooden table holds apples, pears, grapes, several vegetables, and a glass of milk, all showing natural sugar in plant foods and milk. Beside them sits a small bowl filled with white sugar crystals, clearly different from the fresh foods.

pages.text: When we eat sugar and starch, our body changes them into a simple sugar called glucose. Glucose is carried by the blood to all parts of the body, and provides the energy that keeps our body parts working. The body needs this glucose to stay alive.
pages.brief: A child eats a piece of fruit in a sunny kitchen. Inside a simple outline of the child's body, tiny bright dots travel along blood vessels to the arms, legs, and head, representing glucose carried through the blood to give energy to body parts.

pages.text: What Happens to Sugar We Eat?
pages.brief: A piece of sweet food sits on a plate, with a simple human body outline nearby. The scene is calm and clear, inviting the viewer to wonder what happens to sugar inside the body after it is eaten.

pages.text: Where Sugar Is Found The body can get all the sugar it needs from naturally sweet and starchy foods. Many processed foods, which are made by machines in factories, are packed with extra sugar. Cakes, cookies, ice cream, and candy are all processed with added sugar in them.
pages.brief: Inside a food factory, machines process cakes, cookies, ice cream, and candy on a conveyor belt. Nearby, fresh natural foods and starchy foods sit on a table, showing that the body can get the sugar it needs from natural foods rather than only processed sweets.

pages.text: Sugar is also added to foods you might not expect, such as processed tomato sauce and ketchup. Many low-fat sauces and salad dressings contain sugar, too, since sugar is often used to replace fat in those foods.
pages.brief: On a kitchen counter, a bottle of ketchup, a jar of tomato sauce, low-fat sauces, and salad dressings stand together. A hand pours sugar into one of the sauces, showing that sugar is added to foods people might not expect.

pages.text: Breakfast cereal can be another source of added sugar because many cereals have colorful sugary treats added to them. Even cereals with plain flakes may have a dusting of sugar to make them taste sweeter. How much sugar is in these breakfast cereals? 1 cup Grams of sugar Shredded Wheat 0g (no frosting) Toasted Oats 1g Corn Flakes 2g Crisp Rice 3g Raisin Bran 18g.
pages.brief: A breakfast table holds several bowls of cereal: plain flakes, toasted oats, crisp rice, raisin bran, and colorful sugary cereal. A light dusting of sugar falls onto some bowls, while a child looks at the different choices before eating.

pages.text: Sugar and Health Remember, people need glucose to stay alive. When someone has too little glucose in their blood, their body does not have the energy it needs. But too much glucose in the blood can also be bad because it can damage the body.
pages.brief: A tired child sits at a table with a plate of food, while a simple body outline shows only a few bright energy dots traveling through the blood. Beside it, another outline shows too many dots crowding the body, suggesting too little and too much glucose.

pages.text: Over a long time, high glucose levels can strain some parts of the body, such as the heart, brain, and eyes, making it hard for them to work as they should. Do You Know? For some people, sweetened drinks are the biggest source of added sugar. Soda pop and fruit-flavored drinks make up almost half of the added sugar in some people’s diets.
pages.brief: Bottles of soda and fruit-flavored drinks stand on a table beside a simple body outline. Inside the outline, the heart, brain, and eyes are shown under pressure, while a person reaches for a sweetened drink.

pages.text: Making Healthy Choices How can people avoid eating too much added sugar? One way is to eat more natural foods such as fresh fruits and vegetables, which have no added sugar. Another way is to eat homemade meals. Food that is cooked at home is often healthier than processed foods.
pages.brief: In a home kitchen, a family prepares a homemade meal with fresh fruits and vegetables on the counter. A plate of home-cooked food sits beside packaged processed foods, showing that choosing natural foods and cooking at home can help people avoid too much added sugar.

pages.text: People can also limit added sugar by choosing healthier options when snacking. For example, plain yogurt sweetened with fresh fruit and nuts is a better option than donuts or cookies.
pages.brief: A bowl of plain yogurt topped with fresh fruit and nuts sits on a kitchen table beside a plate of donuts and cookies. A child reaches toward the yogurt, showing a healthier snack choice compared with sugary treats.

pages.text: Sugar makes food taste sweeter, but eating too much added sugar can harm our health. Natural sugar and starch provide plenty of energy to fuel our bodies and keep us going. Fresh fruits and vegetables not only taste good, they are also good for the body!
pages.brief: Fresh fruits and vegetables are arranged on a table beside a small bowl of sugar. A child smiles while holding a piece of fruit, showing that natural sugar and starch provide energy and that fresh foods taste good and are good for the body.

books.title: Electric Eels!
books.art_why: Electric eels are living animals that exist today and can be photographed in South American waters.

pages.text: Electric Eels! Found in the murky waters of South America, electric eels are fascinating creatures that continue to intrigue scientists. Electric Eels! provides students with a detailed look at these unique animals and the science behind their shocking abilities.
pages.brief: A long gray-brown electric eel with a yellow-orange throat glides through murky green-brown river water in South America, its body half hidden in the cloudy water, tail curling behind it as it swims past sunken leaves and tangled roots.

pages.text: Legendary Shocker Alexander Humboldt went to South America to catch electric eels in 1800. He thought they could help him learn about electricity, a kind of energy that scientists knew little about. He knew not to touch the eels because their shocks could cause great pain. He asked some fishermen to help.
pages.brief: In 1800 a bearded explorer, Alexander Humboldt, stands on a South American riverbank talking with a small group of fishermen, pointing toward the water where electric eels live, while the fishermen hold nets and listen to his request for help.

pages.text: The fishermen led about thirty horses into a pond. The electric eels began to shock the horses. When the eels were too tired to shock the horses anymore, the fishermen caught five eels. Humboldt learned much about the eels. Shocking Fish Story Recently, a scientist saw eels rise up to protect themselves as they did with the horses. Before that, some scientists thought Humboldt might not have been telling the truth.
pages.brief: Fishermen wade into a shallow pond driving about thirty horses ahead of them through the muddy water, while long electric eels below the surface shock the horses; the tired horses stand in the pond and the fishermen lift five eels out in their nets.

pages.text: It’s a Fish! Electric eels are long gray-brown fish with yellow or orange on their throats. They are more like catfish than other eels and belong to a group of fish that are all electric. Electric eels can be about as big around as an adult person’s leg and three times as long. Male and female electric eels are alike in color and size. Electric Eel Facts Scientific Name Electrophorus electricus Animal Type Fish Diet Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians Length 2 to 3 meters (7–10 feet) Weight 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 pounds)
pages.brief: Two long gray-brown electric eels float side by side in clear water, yellow-orange throats showing; beside them an adult person's leg shows how thick an eel's body is, and the eel stretches about three times longer than that leg.

pages.text: Unlike most other fish, electric eels breathe air. They have gills, but their gills mostly help them breathe out. Electric eels have special organs in their mouths that help them breathe in. They breathe out waste air from their mouths and gills. They come up to breathe air every few minutes and can drown if they don’t.
pages.brief: An electric eel rises to the surface of a slow river with its mouth open, taking in air; its gills at the sides of its head push waste air back out into the water. Other fish swim below, staying underwater, while the eel comes up again.

pages.text: Like most other fish, electric eels have fins and a backbone. Their backbones and fins are body parts that help them move. They swim slowly most of the time, but they move quickly when they attack. Shocking Fact Electric eels can grow new tails if theirs are cut off.
pages.brief: An electric eel swims slowly through calm water, its long fin rippling along its body and its backbone showing through its skin; a second view shows the same eel darting forward fast, jaws open, ready to attack a small fish.

pages.text: It’s Electric! Electric eels are the most electric fish on Earth. They can find their way around and send signals to other eels using their electricity. They can also protect themselves, hunt, and stun or kill the animals they eat. Other fish use electricity, too, but none are as powerful as electric eels. Shocking Medical History Don’t try this at home! Ancient Greeks and Romans tried to cure headaches with electric rays. A ray’s shock could have made a person’s head numb, so it might have worked! Other Electric Fish.
pages.brief: An electric eel sends faint sparks of electricity into dark river water, feeling its way past plants and signalling to another eel nearby; a small fish ahead of it is stunned, while other kinds of electric fish swim in the background, smaller and less powerful.

pages.text: Three organs make an electric eel’s shocks. These organs make up most of an electric eel’s body. They make its body like a big battery that could turn on a light. 1 Shocking Fact If an electric eel curls its head to its 2 tail, its shocking power becomes greater. Three Electric Organs.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of an electric eel shows three long organs packed inside its body, filling most of it, like a battery that could switch on a lamp; beside it the eel curls its head around to touch its tail, its body bent in a tight loop.

pages.text: An electric eel can shock its prey, or the animals it eats, with up to 650 volts of electricity. The shock can kill small animals and stun big ones. Any animal near the eel can feel it. The shock has about five times the volts used to power a lamp. Scientists don’t know why electric eels can’t feel their own shocks. It might be because of how big the eels are. It might be because of how their shock moves. Or it might be because electric eels have body parts that protect them. Electric eels have long rows of special cells called electrocytes. Electrocytes each send out a tiny shock at almost the same time. The cells work together to create the electric eel’s big attack ZAP!
pages.brief: An electric eel snaps its head forward and zaps a small fish with a burst of electricity, long rows of tiny cells inside its body all firing at once; a lamp beside it shows the comparison of power, and the stunned fish hangs in the water.

pages.text: Stunning Attack Before an electric eel uses its attack zap, it has to find prey. Electric eels can’t see well and are nocturnal, or most active at night. Electric eels send out small shocks—about fifty every second—to sense nearby plants and animals. When an electric eel senses prey, it sends out two or three big shocks. The shocks make the prey move, which helps the eel find it quickly. Then the electric eel sends out its attack shock, which stuns or kills the prey. The electric eel sucks the prey into its belly before the animal swims away. Electric eels mostly eat small fish or animals like frogs or shrimp. Young eels also eat worms and insects.
pages.brief: At night in dark river water an electric eel hunts, sending out small steady shocks to sense plants and animals around it; when it finds a frog and a shrimp it releases big shocks, then sucks the stunned prey into its mouth while worms and insects drift nearby.

pages.text: Don’t Swim There! Electric eels are top predators that few other animals eat in the South American rivers where they live. They can also live in other types of nearby fresh water, such as ponds. Because they breathe air, electric eels can live in water that might kill other fish. They can also live out of water for hours if they stay wet. Electric Eel Habitat ATLANTIC OCEAN SOUTH AMERICA PACIFIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: A map shows South America lying between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, with rivers marked where electric eels live; beside it an eel swims in a still pond as the top predator there, with no larger animal hunting it in the murky freshwater.

pages.text: Electric eels mostly lay eggs in small ponds. Male eels build bubble nests with their spit. Female eels lay eggs in the bubbles. Males protect the nest. They also protect the babies until they grow to about half as long as a pencil. The young eels only make small shocks, so they can become prey for other animals.
pages.brief: In a small pond a male electric eel spits bubbles to build a floating nest; a female lays her eggs among the bubbles and the male hovers over them, guarding the tiny young eels that are only about half as long as a pencil.

pages.text: Future Energy Source Scientists are still learning new things about electric eels. Some scientists want to use what they have learned about electric eels to make a new kind of battery. The battery could be used inside people, and it wouldn’t harm them or run out of power. Two hundred years ago, Humboldt wrote that scientists didn’t understand all the secrets of electric fish. That is still true today. What will electric eels help scientists learn next?
pages.brief: Scientists in a laboratory study electric eels in a tank, sketching and taking notes beside a battery they hope to build; an old portrait of Humboldt and his notebook rest on the table as they wonder what the eels will teach them next.

books.title: King George III
books.art_why: A named famous person’s life is best shown in cartoon style for a children’s biography.

pages.text: England, Ireland, and Scotland King George III’s mental health has been the subject of many plays and books, but there’s much more to his story. Learn more about this monarch’s life with this fascinating book.
pages.brief: King George III stands in a grand British royal room, with symbols for England, Ireland, and Scotland around him. Nearby are books and a theater curtain, hinting at the plays and books about his mental health, while the scene introduces his life as a monarch.

pages.text: Meeting George III John Adams, one of America’s first leaders, traveled to England and stood before King George III. The year was 1785, and Adams had the difficult task of making peace between the two countries. America had recently won its freedom in a war against Great Britain. Adams spoke with the king, offering America’s friendship. He spoke highly of the king and wished him good health and happiness. The king smiled. George III may have lost the American colonies, but he knew he would make Great Britain strong again.
pages.brief: In an English royal room in 1785, John Adams, one of America’s first leaders, stands before King George III. Adams offers America’s friendship and speaks highly of the king. The king smiles, knowing he may have lost the American colonies but would make Great Britain strong again.

pages.text: Early Life King George III was born on June 4, 1738. His father and mother were the Prince and Princess of Wales. His grandfather, King George II, was the king of England. Young George grew up in an unhappy family. His father, Frederick, was first in line to be king. Frederick argued with his father, the king. George disliked hearing his father and grandfather fight. Then, at just twelve years old, George’s father died, making George first in line to the British throne. Someday, he would be king.
pages.brief: Young George, a royal boy, stands unhappy in a palace as his father Frederick argues with his grandfather King George II. George dislikes hearing them fight. After his father dies when George is twelve, the boy stands first in line to the British throne.

pages.text: To prepare to be king, George studied harder. Lord Bute, a nobleman, taught George about how British government worked. As king, George would have a ministry, or group of advisors. Another group, called Parliament, made laws for the nation. The king and Parliament often disagreed. George would need to know how to solve problems. In 1760, George’s grandfather died, and George became king of Great Britain and Ireland at the age of twenty-two. At the time, Britain was fighting France and other countries in a European battle called the Seven Years’ War. Soon the war spread to North America.
pages.brief: George studies with Lord Bute, a nobleman, learning how British government, a ministry of advisors, and Parliament make laws. In 1760, after his grandfather dies, George becomes king of Great Britain and Ireland at twenty-two while Britain fights France and other countries in the Seven Years’ War.

pages.text: A Huge Empire In North America, the war was called the French and Indian War. Great Britain was already powerful, but when they defeated the French in North America and in Europe, they controlled more land than ever before. The war caused fighting between Lord Bute and William Pitt, one of the king’s ministers. Pitt wanted to keep fighting, but Bute didn’t. The king sided with Lord Bute and gave him the top job in his ministry. From there, Bute brought an end to the war in 1763 and quit his position shortly after that. North American British Territories in 1763.
pages.brief: After Great Britain defeats the French and controls more land, King George III stands with Lord Bute and William Pitt as the two ministers argue about the French and Indian War. Pitt wants to keep fighting; Bute does not. The king sides with Bute, who ends the war in 1763 and then quits.

pages.text: A Royal Family of His Own Not long after becoming king, George married German princess Sophia Charlotte in 1761. Their marriage lasted for more than fifty years, and they had fifteen children. Happy at home, the king continued to learn all he could and studied more about history and government. He learned the names of all the ships in the Royal Navy. He took his job as king seriously, and he faced big problems. Simple Tastes Even though he was from a royal family, King George enjoyed simpler things. He loved agriculture and spent many days inspecting his kingdom’s farms. His favorite activities included horseback riding, music, attending the theater, and playing cards.
pages.brief: King George III and German princess Sophia Charlotte stand together with their fifteen children in a happy royal home after their 1761 marriage. The king studies history and government, learns Royal Navy ship names, and enjoys simple things: inspecting farms, horseback riding, music, theater, and cards.

pages.text: Trouble in America The British colonies in America challenged the king more than any others. A huge problem there was about to begin. Great Britain needed money to pay bills from the Seven Years’ War. To get money, England taxed items bought by the colonists. Colonists now had to pay taxes on molasses, printed paper, paint, glass, and tea. They became angry and refused to buy British goods. To protest the taxes, they planned the Boston Tea Party. One night in 1773, a group of colonists climbed aboard a British ship carrying tea in Boston Harbor. The colonists dumped the tea into the water below.
pages.brief: Angry American colonists refuse British goods after England taxes molasses, printed paper, paint, glass, and tea to pay Seven Years’ War bills. One night in 1773, a group of colonists climbs aboard a British ship carrying tea in Boston Harbor and dumps the tea into the water below.

pages.text: The colonists’ actions angered the king. Soon the tensions boiled over into war. For Great Britain to win, King George realized he needed more fighting men. He hired a group of German soldiers to help in the fight. Thirty thousand Germans fought next to British troops against the American colonists. The American Revolution went on for seven years. The Americans won the war in 1781. The king said the defeat was not his fault.
pages.brief: The colonists’ actions anger King George III. Tensions boil over into war, and the king hires thirty thousand German soldiers to fight next to British troops against the American colonists. The American Revolution lasts seven years until the Americans win in 1781. The king says the defeat is not his fault.

pages.text: In the years after the American Revolution, the king started acting strangely. He seemed nervous all the time, said odd things, and was confused. He shouted at others and pushed them. Doctors helped the king using the latest treatments. Over time, the king seemed to get better. He returned to his leadership role.
pages.brief: After the American Revolution, King George III acts strangely: he seems nervous, says odd things, is confused, and shouts at and pushes others. Doctors help the king using the latest treatments. Over time he seems to get better and returns to his leadership role.

pages.text: More Conflicts King George soon faced more challenges, including another war with France. By 1799, France had a new leader—Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon wanted to take over Europe, including Great Britain. King George did not want to lose his country. Great Britain and France fought until 1815, when France lost the war. At the same time, a fight started in Ireland. People there felt that Great Britain passed unfair religious laws. The Irish started a rebellion, but Great Britain defeated them.
pages.brief: King George III faces another war with France. By 1799, France’s new leader Napoleon Bonaparte wants to take over Europe, including Great Britain. The king does not want to lose his country, and Great Britain fights France until 1815, when France loses. At the same time, Great Britain defeats an Irish rebellion over unfair religious laws.

pages.text: Later Years King George III was in his fiftieth year as king in 1809, and the country celebrated. The joy would not last long, however. In 1810, the king’s youngest daughter died, which left George heartbroken. George again became mentally and physically ill. The king was unable to finish his royal duties. Parliament allowed Prince George, his son, to rule Great Britain in 1811. In January 1820, King George III died, and his son became King George IV.
pages.brief: In 1809, the country celebrates King George III’s fiftieth year as king, but the joy does not last. In 1810 his youngest daughter dies, leaving him heartbroken and mentally and physically ill. Parliament lets his son Prince George rule in 1811. In January 1820 the king dies, and his son becomes King George IV.

pages.text: New Opinions During his time in power, King George III lost the war with America and slowly became mentally ill. For a long time, many historians thought he was a bad king. Recently, they have changed their opinions of him. George III won two major wars—the Seven Years’ War and the wars with Napoleon. He served as king for sixty years, and he led his country to greatness. Through it all, he remained a good husband and father, and he always put his country first.
pages.brief: Historians once thought King George III was a bad king because he lost the war with America and slowly became mentally ill. Recently they have changed their opinions: he won the Seven Years’ War and the wars with Napoleon, served sixty years, led his country to greatness, and remained a good husband and father who put his country first.

pages.text: The Life of George III.
pages.brief: King George III is shown in a royal portrait inside a grand British palace room. He wears royal robes and stands with a serious expression. The picture represents the life of this British monarch, George III.

books.title: April Fools' Day
books.art_why: The book mixes ancient, medieval, and modern scenes, so drawings can show every period and prank clearly.

pages.text: Have your friends ever tried to convince you to buy some plaid paint? If so, you’ve probably been the victim of an April Fools’ Day prank! April Fools’ Day is a fascinating book that delves into the history of April Fools’ Day and.
pages.brief: Two friends stand together, one holding a can of plaid-patterned paint, the other looking unsure. Nearby, a book lies open with small illustrated scenes of history, world celebrations, famous jokes, companies, and online pranks, suggesting the many kinds of April Fools' Day foolery.

pages.text: Pranking Fun It’s early spring. Your chili ends up buried under a pile of salt. You’re the victim of an April Fools’ joke. April Fools’ Day is on or near April 1. It’s the one day of the year to play jokes, or pranks, on people.
pages.brief: In early spring, a child sits at a table and discovers a bowl of chili buried under a huge pile of salt. Friends hide nearby, ready to laugh, while the child realizes the surprise is an April Fools' Day prank.

pages.text: A common joke may be replacing the sugar with salt. When people see that it’s a joke, yell “April Fools’!”
pages.brief: At a kitchen table, one person spoons white salt into a sugar bowl while another sips a drink and grimaces. The prankster grins, and the surprised person shouts with a laugh once the joke is clear.

pages.text: Why April First? No one knows why April Fools’ Day is on April 1. It may once have marked the coming of spring. People were often “fooled” by the changing weather at this time of the year. Another idea is that April Fools’ Day began when we first started using the calendar we use today. The start of the new year moved from the beginning of April to January 1. People who still celebrated New Year’s Day on April 1 were called “April fools.” Gotham Goes Mad One story tells how April Fools’ may have started in the English town of Gotham. King John planned to take villagers’ property. The villagers acted like they suffered from insanity to scare King John away. In those days, insanity was thought to be contagious.
pages.brief: In the English town of Gotham, villagers pretend to be insane—dancing, shouting, and acting wild—while King John and his guards back away, fearing insanity is contagious. Nearby, spring weather shifts from sunshine to snow, and a turning calendar hints at the new year moving from April to January.

pages.text: Many celebrations were held in the past near April 1. The ancient Romans celebrated the longer days of spring. They dressed in costumes and played jokes. In Europe in the twelfth century, people celebrated the Feast of Fools. A fake ruler led followers in a parade. People celebrated in this way until the sixteenth century.
pages.brief: In ancient Rome, people in costumes celebrate the longer spring days with playful jokes. In a twelfth-century European town, a fake ruler leads a lively parade of followers during the Feast of Fools, with smiling crowds celebrating together.

pages.text: Around the World Today, people celebrate April Fools’ Day the world. Scottish Scramble In Scotland, April Fools’ can go on for two days. On April 1, people in Scotland send friends on foolish tasks. The second day is for playing more jokes. Tips to Avoid Being the April Fool! • Have you read it carefully? Do you really believe there is a cross between a sheep and a pig called a “shig?” • Do you get the feeling you’re being watched? Be on your guard! • Careful! That present may not be what you think.
pages.brief: In a Scottish town, a smiling prankster sends a friend off on a silly errand while others hide and watch. A wrapped present sits nearby, and a strange sheep-pig creature peeks from behind a hedge, adding to the playful tricks.

pages.text: French Foolishness In France, April 1 is called “April Fish.” The fish is a person who is easily fooled. People tape paper fish to each other’s backs.
pages.brief: On a French street, people smile and chat while paper fish are taped to their backs. One person walks on, unaware of the paper fish fluttering behind, as friends quietly enjoy the April Fish joke.

pages.text: American Tricksters In the United States, the fun lasts all day. Tell a friend that class is canceled or punch holes in his or her water bottle! Other jokes may be to put oil on a doorknob and food color in milk. You may find plastic bugs in food or on your bed. Brazil’s Day of the Lie In Brazil, April 1 is Dia da mentira (Lie Day). People enjoy playing practical jokes, or brincadeiras (breen-kah- DAY-rahs), on each other and tell silly lies all day.
pages.brief: In a U.S. classroom, a child grins while telling a friend that class is canceled; a water bottle has tiny holes, milk is oddly colored, and plastic bugs sit on a bed. In Brazil, people laugh and trade silly lies during Lie Day.

pages.text: Jordanian Jokesters On April 1, 2010, a newspaper in Jordan had an interesting front- page story. It reported that three spaceships had landed in the desert nearby. Some people in the town were not used to April Fools’ pranks and got scared. The newspaper apologized for the story. Sizdah Bedar The Iranian (Persian) calendar is very old. The thirteenth day of the Iranian new year is called Sizdah Bedar (seez-DAH be-DAR). It falls around April 1 and has been around since 536 bc. On Sizdah Bedar, families and friends share picnics, pranks, and fun. It might just be the oldest-known joke day in history.
pages.brief: In a Jordanian town, people look frightened by a startling report that three spaceships landed in the nearby desert. In Iran, families and friends share a picnic with playful pranks and fun, celebrating Sizdah Bedar around the same time of year.

pages.text: Famous Foolery Some April Fools’ jokes are famous. Spaghetti Trees? In 1957, a British TV show described a spaghetti tree. When the show was over, many people called the station wanting one.
pages.brief: In a 1957 British television studio, a presenter gestures toward a tree hung with strands of spaghetti. Afterward, many viewers crowd telephone lines, calling the station to ask for a spaghetti tree of their own.

pages.text: Corporate Chaos Companies and the media fool people, too. On April 1, 1996, Taco Bell said that it had bought the American Liberty Bell. The company said it would now be called the “Taco Liberty Bell.” Many people believed the story. The company had to say it was a joke. In 1998, Burger King showed an ad for a left-handed burger. They said it made left-handed eating easier.
pages.brief: A fast-food spokesperson stands beside the American Liberty Bell, claiming it as a company purchase, while startled people believe the story. Nearby, a Burger King advertisement shows a left-handed burger being eaten easily by a smiling customer.

pages.text: Online Pranks Internet April Fools’ jokes spread fast. One of Google’s famous jokes was a drink it said made people smarter. In 2012, a radio station said that Twitter was changing to 133 characters per tweet. It was a joke. In 2013, Twitter said it would ask people who used vowels in their tweets to pay more. This, too, was a joke. Even Pokémon Go began as an Internet joke in 2014. Google Maps said it had a tool that would find the best Pokémon Master in the world.
pages.brief: Around computers and phones, people chuckle as online pranks spread: a colorful drink promises to make people smarter, a social media bird shrinks a message bar to a tiny size, and a map screen searches for a Pokémon Master.

pages.text: Conclusion Follow certain rules during April Fools’ Day. Don’t be mean. If you’re going to make a joke, make sure you can take a joke in return. Many places around the world enjoy April Fools’ Day. Keep it safe and fun!
pages.brief: Children from different places share a laugh after a harmless April Fools' prank, making sure everyone is smiling and no one is upset. They stand together in a bright, friendly group, keeping the joke safe and fun.

books.title: Itching and Scratching
books.art_why: The book covers real skin, insects, plants, animals, and medical treatments that can be photographed today.

pages.text: When you feel an itch, your body’s internal system is sending a signal to protect you from sickness. Itching and Scratching is a nonfiction text that informs students about the reasons we itch and how to prevent scratching.
pages.brief: A person's skin shows an itch while a simplified internal signal travels through the body, warning of possible sickness and showing the body's protective system at work. The focus is on the skin and the internal signal, with a plain background.

pages.text: Tickle, Touch, Scratch It starts with a tickle. You brush your hand against your skin, but the tickle continues. You can’t help but scratch. Ahh, relief, but it lasts just a moment. Then the feeling returns, even stronger. Before long, you’re scratching away again. We’ve all had that experience. There are dozens of reasons for itching, and there’s a good explanation for why scratching seems to relieve an itch.
pages.brief: A person brushes a hand against their skin and keeps feeling a tickle, then scratches and shows brief relief before the itch returns stronger. The person scratches again, illustrating a common itch-scratch experience with a simple explanation focus.

pages.text: More Than Skin-Deep When you think of itching, you usually think of skin. It’s true that itching happens mostly on your skin. After all, skin covers your whole body. Skin is also the only thing that stands between the inside of your body and the outside world. All sorts of things touch your skin. Skin has nerve cells that react when something touches it. Some of those things are harmless. Some, however, are harmful or even dangerous. An itch is your body’s way of warning that these things can hurt you. For example, many people are allergic to poison ivy. This plant has irritating oils that rub off on skin. The oils make skin blister and ooze. Open blisters can get infected. The oils can also affect other parts of the body, like the nose and lungs. Contact with poison ivy can cause a bad infection to develop.
pages.brief: Skin covers the whole body and stands between the inside and outside world. Nerve cells in the skin react to touch, and a person's skin shows poison ivy oils causing blisters that ooze, with open blisters at risk of infection and effects on the nose and lungs.

pages.text: Your body uses itching to keep infections from happening. Itching is a signal from your immune system—your body’s internal system that helps protect you from sickness. When you touch poison ivy, your immune system triggers an itch. This informs you that your skin has touched something harmful. In this case, the itch teaches you to stay away from poison ivy. The Itch-Scratch Cycle.
pages.brief: A person touches poison ivy, and the body's immune system triggers an itch as a warning signal. The scene shows the harmful plant contact on the skin and the itch teaching the person to stay away, with the itch-scratch cycle implied.

pages.text: Causes of Itching It’s not just your skin that itches. Your eyes can feel itchy, too, and so can your nose and throat. Scratching is a reflex action to itching—something you do automatically, or without thinking. However, you can’t reach down your throat to scratch it, so you cough. You can’t scratch inside your nose, so you sneeze. Scratching your eyes can cause damage, so you rub them instead. All those actions have the same goal: to remove whatever is causing the itch. Perhaps you ate something spicy. Maybe you breathed dust or got smoke in your eyes. A good cough, sneeze, or rub could get rid of the problem!
pages.brief: A person feels itching in the eyes, nose, and throat. Since the throat cannot be scratched, the person coughs; since the nose cannot be scratched inside, the person sneezes; and the person rubs itchy eyes. Spicy food, dust, or smoke may be the cause.

pages.text: Sometimes, though, you can’t get rid of the cause of your itch easily. Sometimes the cause comes from a germ inside your body. The itch you feel may be part of a sickness caused by the germ. Chicken pox is a sickness caused by a virus. The virus makes the skin break out in very itchy blisters. Today, many children get a vaccine to prevent them from getting chicken pox. Luckily, for those who do get sick, chicken pox is a temporary condition. After a while, the sickness passes.
pages.brief: A child's skin shows itchy blisters from chicken pox, a sickness caused by a virus inside the body. The scene shows the temporary condition breaking out on the skin, with a vaccine preventing many children from getting chicken pox and the sickness passing after a while.

pages.text: There are other itchy conditions, though, that last much longer. These are known as chronic conditions. Some just affect the skin. Others cause different parts of the body to itch. One chronic condition, psoriasis, speeds up the life cycle of skin cells. The cells build up on the surface and form itchy scales. Another condition, eczema, is a rash that is common in children but can occur in people at any age. Chronic conditions have no cure. People who suffer from them can do some things to help, though. For instance, they can avoid using skin care products that may cause the condition to flare up.
pages.brief: A person's skin shows chronic itchy conditions: psoriasis causes skin cells to build up into itchy scales, while eczema appears as a rash common in children and possible at any age. The scene shows the long-lasting skin conditions and the need to avoid skin care products that cause flare-ups.

pages.text: Insect bites, especially mosquito bites, are another common cause of itching. Female mosquitos feast on blood. Their bites can introduce dangerous germs to your bloodstream. Mosquitos can spread serious diseases, such as malaria and dengue fever. Fortunately, their bite causes your body to itch almost immediately. The itch catches your attention and makes you swat the insect away to protect yourself from even more bites. In this case, an itch can be a real lifesaver!
pages.brief: A female mosquito bites a person's skin and feeds on blood, introducing germs that can spread diseases such as malaria and dengue fever. The bite causes an immediate itch, and the person swats the insect away, showing how the itch helps protect against more bites.

pages.text: Nervous System It’s a Real Pain... or Is It? People once thought that itching was a form of pain. It isn’t. It does have a relationship with pain, though. That relationship is why scratching helps relieve itching. Your body has a network of nerves that feel all sorts of sensations. Nerves that sense itching overlap with nerves that feel pain. Nerves can only sense one feeling at a time. Unlike itching, scratching is a form of pain. When you apply pain by scratching, coughing, or rubbing, the painful feeling blocks the itch. For some people, the pain is almost pleasant because it stops the misery of itching.
pages.brief: A network of nerves in the body senses itching and pain, with the two kinds of nerves overlapping. A person scratches the skin, and the painful feeling of scratching blocks the itch because nerves can sense only one feeling at a time, sometimes making the pain feel almost pleasant.

pages.text: Too much scratching can cause problems. If you scratch until you bleed, you set yourself up for infection. Scratching blisters can leave scars. Constantly rubbing your eyes can hurt them. A coughing fit makes it hard to catch your breath. Creepy Crawlies One of the creepiest sources of itching is the mango fly of Africa. This insect may lay eggs on clothes hung out to dry. When the eggs hatch, the larvae burrow under the skin of the person wearing the infected clothes. The larvae cause serious itching until they mature and burst out from sores on the skin.
pages.brief: A person scratches skin until it bleeds, showing how too much scratching can lead to infection, scars, hurt eyes, or trouble breathing. A mango fly from Africa lays eggs on clothes hung out to dry, and larvae burrow under a person's skin, causing serious itching until they burst out from sores on the skin.

pages.text: Oh, What a Relief! Scratching temporarily relieves itching, but it’s not a good long-term solution. For chronic itching, you need lasting relief. The best solution, of course, is to remove the cause of the itch. Sometimes, though, that is not possible. Lotions and creams can offer some relief, and so can eyedrops. These are topical medicines, which means they are applied to the surface of the body. Topical medicines that soothe itches. Some people have even found relief by taking a bath in oatmeal!
pages.brief: A person applies lotion or cream to itchy skin, showing topical medicine applied to the body's surface for relief. The scene includes eyedrops for itchy eyes and a bath in oatmeal, presenting ways to soothe itching when the cause cannot be removed and lasting relief is needed.

pages.text: For severe itching, you may have to take oral medicines. These come in the form of pills, capsules, or liquids that you swallow. Oral medicines block or lessen your body’s response to whatever causes an itch. The urge to scratch goes away. Itchy Critters Animals scratch for many of the same reasons humans do. But there’s another reason that animals scratch: they need to molt. Molting means shedding fur, feathers, or skin as the animal grows or as the seasons change. Furry animals shed hair. Birds lose feathers. Reptiles such as snakes crawl out of their old skin. Scratching speeds the process along. Animals may rub against trees or rocks to get rid of their old layers.
pages.brief: A person takes oral medicine in pill, capsule, or liquid form to lessen the body's itch response, and the urge to scratch goes away. Nearby, furry animals shed hair, a bird loses feathers, and a snake crawls out of old skin, with animals rubbing against trees or rocks to remove old layers.

pages.text: Itch, Scratch, Learn Feeling itchy isn’t fun, but think of it as a safety mechanism. It’s part of your body’s amazing defense system. Itching lets you know what is bad for you and teaches you to avoid it. The next time you feel itchy, ask yourself why—before you scratch. Learning what makes you itch and avoiding it is the best way to keep from getting itchy again! Things You Can Do If you have troublesome itching, there are some things you can do that may relieve it and prevent damage caused by scratching. These include: • patting or tapping the itchy area rather than scratching it. • holding a cold, damp cloth against the itchy area to cool it down. • washing in cool or lukewarm water. • using nonperfumed skin care products. • avoiding wearing clothes that irritate your skin, such as wool or polyester. • applying a cream to dry or flaky skin.
pages.brief: A person treats itchy skin as a safety warning from the body's defense system, patting the area instead of scratching and holding a cold, damp cloth against it. The scene also shows cool washing, nonperfumed products, non-irritating clothes, and cream for dry or flaky skin.

books.title: Treasure Found
books.art_why: The book profiles named famous treasure hunters such as Howard Carter and Mel Fisher.

pages.text: Treasure Found is a book about different types of treasures found throughout time. It names famous treasure hunters and their finds, such as Howard Carter and the tomb of King Tut; and Mel Fisher, who found underwater treasures worth millions of dollars.
pages.brief: A collage of treasures from different times: gold and gems from King Tut's tomb, underwater treasure, and a treasure hunter's map. Howard Carter stands by the tomb of King Tut, and Mel Fisher is shown with sunken treasure worth millions of dollars.

pages.text: INTRODUCTION On Saturday morning, you are busy cleaning your room. Under your bed, you discover a box. You look inside. You see a plastic ring, a birthday card with a dollar inside, a shell, and a postcard from a friend. You say, “Wow! I forgot about this stuff.” You have just found treasure.
pages.brief: On a Saturday morning, a child cleans a bedroom and finds a box under the bed. Inside are a plastic ring, a birthday card with a dollar inside, a shell, and a postcard from a friend. The child smiles and says, 'Wow! I forgot about this stuff.'

pages.text: TREASURE HUNTING Treasure is anything that someone thinks is valuable. Over the years, much treasure has been found. In 1922, Howard Carter found gold and gems in the tomb of ancient Egypt’s King Tutankhamun. In 1874, Heinrich Schliemann dug up an ancient Greek city. In 1964, Robert Marx found a city, too, under the sea near the island of Jamaica. He also discovered thousands of silver coins.
pages.brief: Howard Carter stands inside King Tutankhamun's tomb beside gold and gems. Heinrich Schliemann digs at an ancient Greek city. Robert Marx dives near Jamaica, where he finds a sunken city and thousands of silver coins. Around them are valuable treasures from different times.

pages.text: In Florida, Kip Wagner picked up some Spanish coins called “pieces of eight,” which had washed up on the shore. He knew they had come from a shipwreck. He started to search the ocean floor. He wanted to find the shipwreck. Over time, he found sunken treasure worth millions of dollars.
pages.brief: Kip Wagner kneels on a Florida beach, picking up Spanish coins washed up on the shore. He knows they came from a shipwreck. He dives and searches the ocean floor, and over time he finds sunken treasure worth millions of dollars.

pages.text: SUNKEN TREASURE Sunken treasure is especially hard to find because it is under water. Yet, people continue to search for treasure deep under the sea. A Spanish ship called the Atocha (ah-TOH-cha) held one of the most famous sunken treasures. In 1622, a group of Spanish ships, including the Atocha, took on a cargo of gold, silver, coins, and gems. The ships left Havana, Cuba, headed for Spain. They sailed into the path of a great storm. The Atocha and several of the other ships in the group sank near the Florida Keys.
pages.brief: Spanish ships, including the Atocha, leave Havana, Cuba, carrying gold, silver, coins, and gems. They head for Spain. A great storm strikes, and the Atocha and several other ships sink near the Florida Keys, with treasure still aboard.

pages.text: Spain sent ships to find the cargo from the sunken shipwrecks. Divers found the cannon from the Santa Margarita, one of the ships from the group. They could not find anything else because another storm had broken up that ship. They did not find any sign of the Atocha.
pages.brief: Spanish divers search the wreck area and find a cannon from the Santa Margarita, one of the ships in the group. Another storm has broken up that ship, so they find nothing else. They see no sign of the Atocha.

pages.text: MEL FISHER AND THE ATOCHA For years, people dreamed of finding the Atocha. Mel Fisher dreamed of it, too. As a boy, he had read Treasure Island, the story of a young man who went looking for pirate treasure. Mel wanted to find lost treasure. Luckily, he liked diving under the sea. He even owned a dive shop. In the early 1960s, Mel Fisher decided to look for the Atocha. Friends and family, wife, sons, and joined in the search. People gave him money to help with the search. Everyone would share the the Atocha was found.
pages.brief: As a boy, Mel Fisher reads an adventure book about pirate treasure and dreams of finding lost treasure. As an adult, he works in his dive shop and plans a search for the Atocha. His wife, sons, friends, and helpers join the search.

pages.text: For several years, Mel and his crew searched the ocean. They used metal detectors and sonar to find pieces of the ship on the seafloor. Sonar can find things deep under the water that cannot be seen. Mel and his crew found many things, including other shipwrecks, but not the Atocha. Do You Know? Sonar uses sound to find objects under the water. A sound wave is sent out. When it hits an object it bounces back to the sensor. The sonar echoes are used to form an image.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher and his crew search the ocean from a boat, using metal detectors and sonar. Underwater, sound waves from the sonar bounce off objects and form images. They find pieces of ships and other shipwrecks on the seafloor, but not the Atocha.

pages.text: Florida GULF OF Florida MEXICO Florida Keys X MARKS THE SPOT In 1970, Mel and his crew got help from a friend named Eugene Lyon. He looked through old books about Spanish ships. In them, he read the Atocha ’s cargo list and clues to where the ship could be found. He told Mel that he had been looking in the wrong place!
pages.brief: Eugene Lyon studies old books about Spanish ships and finds clues about the Atocha's cargo and where the ship could be. He tells Mel Fisher that the crew has been looking in the wrong place. A chart of Florida and the Gulf lies nearby.

pages.text: Mel and his crew sailed one hundred miles from where they had been looking to a new place. Three years later, they found silver bars with markings they had not seen before. These markings matched the Atocha ’s cargo list. Now they knew they were near the treasure. Still, two years later, they had not found the ship. Then, tragedy struck. Mel’s son, Dirk; Dirk’s wife, Angel; and a diver, Rick Gage, drowned when their search boat overturned in the ocean.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher and his crew sail one hundred miles to a new search area. They find silver bars with unfamiliar markings that match the Atocha's cargo list, so they know treasure is near. Later, their search boat overturns in the ocean, and the crew grieves for Dirk, Angel, and Rick Gage, who drowned.

pages.text: Mel was saddened by the loss, but he decided to continue the search. For ten more years, he and his crew searched for the remains of the ship. In 1985, Mel and his crew finally found the cargo hold of the Atocha. The treasure included gold and silver worth millions of dollars. Mel and his crew marked where everything had been found. They took pictures, too. They wrote down information for historians who might want to study what happened to the ship.
pages.brief: Mel Fisher is sad but continues the search for ten more years. In 1985, he and his crew find the cargo hold of the Atocha, filled with gold and silver worth millions. On the boat, they mark locations, photograph the finds, and prepare information for historians.

pages.text: The treasure from the Atocha was great and very valuable. Mel gave a part of the treasure to the state of Florida. He also gave some of the treasure to museums. He shared the rest of the treasure with his family and others who had helped him in his search. He sold some of it, too. Today, you can visit the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Society and Museum in Florida. You can see many of the beautiful things he found.
pages.brief: The Atocha treasure is displayed in the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Society and Museum in Florida, where visitors see gold, silver, and beautiful objects. Mel Fisher gave part of the treasure to Florida and museums, shared some with family and helpers, and sold some.

pages.text: CONCLUSION What treasure still waits to be discovered? You could join one of the many treasure- hunting groups around the world. You might discover an ancient city or tomb, or even a sunken or buried chest of gold. You can find many books and websites about treasure and treasure hunting. Maybe you will be the one to find the next great treasure.
pages.brief: A young treasure hunter joins a treasure-hunting group. Around them are imagined finds: an ancient city, a tomb, a sunken ship, and a buried chest of gold. Books and a computer with a treasure-hunting website show where to learn more.
